Q3 2009 TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD Earnings Conference Call - Final https://www.proquest.com/newspapers/q3-2009-tata-consultancy-services-ltd-earnings/docview/466101914/se-2?accountid=27562 Abstract: None available. Full text: OPERATOR: Ladies and gentlemen, good morning and good evening. I am Rochelle, the moderator for this conference call. Welcome to the TCS earnings conference. Please note that for the duration of this presentation, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and this conference is being recorded. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions. (Operator Instructions). At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Mr. Kedar Shirali, Director of Global Investor Relations. Thank you and over to you, Mr. Shirali. KEDAR SHIRALI, DIRECTOR OF IR, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD: Thank you, Rochelle. Good evening and welcome, everyone. Thank you for joining us on TCS' earnings call for the third quarter of fiscal year 2009. I'm Kedar Shirali from Investor Relations. Please note that this call is being webcast through our website and an archive, including the transcript, will be available on the site for the duration of the quarter. The financial statements, results presentation and press releases are also available on our website, www.tcs.com. Our leadership team is present on this call to discuss our results for the quarter. We have with us Mr. S. Ramadorai, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director. S. RAMADORAI, CEO & MANAGING DIRECTOR, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD: Good evening, friends. KEDAR SHIRALI: Mr. S. Mahalingam, Chief Financial Officer and Executive Director. S. MAHALINGAM, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR & CFO, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD: Good morning, good evening. KEDAR SHIRALI: Mr. N. Chandrasekaran, Chief Operating Officer and Executive Director. N. CHANDRASEKARAN, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR & COO, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD: Good morning and good afternoon and good evening. KEDAR SHIRALI: Mr. Phiroz A. Vandrevala, Head of Global Corporate Affairs and Executive Director. PHIROZ VANDREVALA, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR & HEAD OF GLOBAL CORPORATE AFFAIRS, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD: Hi. KEDAR SHIRALI: And Mr. Ajoy Mukherjee, Head of Global Human Resources. AJOY MUKHERJEE, VP & HEAD OF GLOBAL HUMAN RESOURCES, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES LTD: Hello. KEDAR SHIRALI: Ram, Maha and Chandra will each give

you a brief overview of the Company's performance, followed by a Q&A session. As you are aware, TCS does not provide specific revenue and earnings guidance. Let me remind you that anything said on this call which reflects our outlook for the future or which can be construed as a forward-looking statement must be reviewed in conjunction with the risks that the Company faces. These risks are outlined in the second slide of our results presentation, which is uploaded on our website. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Mr. Ramadorai to begin the proceedings. S. RAMADORAI: Thank you, Kedar. 2009 has started much along the lines of how 2008 ended. The global economic scenario has further deteriorated since we last met in October of 2008. In such times, TCS' performance in quarter three has been disciplined and satisfactory. To compare on a year-on-year basis, we have shown a robust performance in terms of growth. The revenues, at INR7,277 crores or $1.483b, have shown a growth of 24.10% in rupee terms. The operational strength of the Company has resulted in good operational performance, with operating profit at INR1,802 crores, up 31.44% over last year. The growth in net profits to INR1,352 crores has been muted because of non-operational factors like rupee [fluency] and the hedging. Our revenue mix of multiple currencies, which Maha will cover, is also to be understood in the overall context. When I come to quarter-on-quarter on a sequential basis, our performance has been good. Revenues for the quarter, at INR7,277 crores or $1.483b, is a growth of 4.65% in rupee terms and 1.23% in terms of constant currency terms. The net profits, at INR1,352 crores, is a growth of 7.21% quarter-on-quarter. We will continue to focus on sustaining long-term growth, balancing growth across vertical -- markets and verticals, improving the productivity of all our resources and ensuring a sustainable margin scenario. [I mean the] situation in such uncertain times, for all of us, is to best look at focusing on improving our own operational efficiencies while ensuring that we continue to focus on

our customers' requirements and then help them through these difficult times. And also, pursue select engagements, which has resulted in adding 41 new clients in quarter three. Our continual drive to increase operational efficiencies is [yielding]. This will continue to be our focus area. And some of the very specific operational highlights have been improving in operating margin by two to three basis points through moving more work offshore, increased productivity, exchange gains and great project execution. The offshore mix per se has improved by 106 basis points. We also reduced our overall debtor days outstanding by nine days in quarter three. In a tough market, TCS continues to play -- display strong pricing discipline and this is reflected in our numbers. Pricing has been stable despite these pressures. We completed, during this quarter, the acquisition of Citi's captive BPO unit and this unit is being integrated into TCS and the revenues will start flowing into TCS from quarter four onwards. The domain-led banking process expertise gives us a unique strategic advantage going forward. It will also allow us to offer banks -- all the banks an outsourcing solution for their core operations and offer this core [domain] intensive BPO. We will have the opportunity to allow our clients to derive much more value from their technology spends in addition to their IT services spends. Looking ahead, new opportunities are emerging slowly in areas like integration activity, as a result of demergers and acquisitions, as well as compliance and regulatory requirements, as well as optimization of technology and operations as customers look to reduce costs and drive back to profitability. We remain on track to achieve our hiring target for the FY '09, which is in excess of 30,000. Our attrition has dropped to 11.9% and we will continue to focus on our employees and capability building. Before I hand over to Chandra to talk about the demand and provide a perspective on operations, I would like to talk about corporate governance, which has become a front burner issue of late for all of us and all of you. TCS

is rooted in strong fundamentals. Our approach is that of institutional building and value creation for our customers and other stakeholders. TCS has always been a role model by adopting the highest level of corporate governance, practices highlighted by the Company's transparency, ethics and integrity, values that flow from the Tata] Group's code of conduct. While we [can't] provide the details, I would like to reiterate that TCS does not believe in fulfilling the requirements of clause 49 of the listing agreement as a mere box-ticking exercise. We consider the quality of our directors to be more important than merely the fact that they are independent. And speaking about transparency and governance, there is one more aspect that I would like to highlight. TCS has been paying dividends every quarter since it went public in August 2004. The dividend paid in the current quarter makes it 18 consecutive quarters that we have paid the dividends. I know that this practice is greatly appreciated by over 7,000 retail investors after -- as well as our institutional investors. Thank you and over to Chandra. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Thanks, Ram. From an operational perspective, I just want to make three or four important points. It has been a tough environment. What started as a slowdown in the BFS sector has really moved on to other sectors, especially manufacturing, high-tech and telecom. Given that, our focus has been execution rigor and pricing discipline. We believe these two are extremely critical, so that we remain efficient and very disciplined to take advantage whenever the opportunities ramp up. In this quarter, we have achieved an offshore movement of 106 basis points and achieved a good volume growth of 2.42% and then maintained our pricing. Second, from a deal perspective, it has been a good quarter. We signed six large deals at least, of which two of them came in the retail sector, one in the BFS sector, one in the utilities sector and one in high-tech and pharma. Out of those deals, one is more than $100m value, another one is more than $250m in value, and

we expect the ramp-ups to start sometime in the Q4. In terms of the sectors where we see opportunities, we see the retail, media, pharma and utility sectors doing better than BFS and manufacturing and high-tech sectors. Going forward, I would like to say that we have a very healthy deal pipeline and we just need to make sure that the closures are happening. And with regard to client budgets, it's still company-specific. There are clients who have worked their budgets out and then have had discussions with us in terms of what their outlook is for 2009 and what projects we are going to do. And there are clients who still are uncertain about what programs they will do. So we're having to manage the business extremely carefully and that's what we are focused on. The other point is, in terms of the constant currency, also, we showed growth this quarter, 123 basis point growth. Thank you and (inaudible) [Maha]. S. MAHALINGAM: Thanks, Chandra. TCS' performance in the third quarter was focused on (inaudible) improvement in an environment, as Ram said, of -- full of uncertainty and turmoil. In this environment, the best bet is to continue the diversification of revenues, move towards sustainable, efficient cost base, improve the collection process, be prudent in cash and currency management and focus on continuing the upward trend. Our operational performance in Q2 has delivered on all these. We recorded revenues, as Ram has already said, of INR7,277 crores, equivalent to US dollars -- $1.48b for the quarter. That's an increase of 4.65% quarter-on-quarter and 24.12% (sic - see presentation) year on year in rupee terms. This has come about through volume increase, a favorable exchange rate and a disciplined approach to maintaining our pricing. Breakdown of revenue growth quarter over -- from -- between last quarter and this is as follows. Volume, 2.2% increase. Pricing has been a drop of 10 basis points. Effort mix, that is movement from onsite to offshore, has had a negative effect on revenue to the extent of 1.06%. Foreign exchange has contributed to 3.39% and

therefore the overall figure is 4.65%. That's the revenue increase. The positive effect of the rupee depreciation against the US dollar was diluted by the relative strengthening of the rupee against other currencies, such as pounds sterling, euro, Australian dollar and Brazilian real, in which about 33.9% of our revenues are denominated. So while, on the total revenue, we got a 5.9% benefit from US dollar appreciation against the rupee, we lost 1.7% as rupee appreciated against British pound sterling and 0.9% against euro. Concerning all currencies other than US dollar and rupee, our revenues were negatively impacted by 2.5%. Netting the two figures, the incremental revenue in INR as a result of currency movement was 3.4%, that is INR2.36b. However, the negative swing against the US dollar also meant that our revenues, when reported in US dollar, have come down by 5.8% in this quarter. To get a true view of our performance without letting currency volatility skew the picture, it will be good to talk in terms of constant currency, based on the rates of the previous quarter. In constant currency terms, we had revenue growth of 1.23%. Cost management continues as a long-term sustained program. By focusing on each item of cost, such as travel, communication, rent, etc., we have been able to achieve a reduction in SG&A of 130 basis points. In addition, we continued to shift work offshore, increasing offshore revenues by 1%. The margin-accretive effect of these profitability levers, lower provisioning for bad and doubtful debts and the favorable currency movement was diluted by lower productivity from the holiday season. Despite that, our operating margin grew by 54 basis points sequentially to 24.76%. This does not mean that we've stopped investing in the business for longer term. Selling activities were not curtailed. Investments continued to be made locally in people, technology, marketing and branding, so TCS can be prepared for the eventual upturn in market conditions and demand for our services as they go up. In addition to continuing the planned recruitment program, we continued our investment in infrastructure. We brought in 5,139 additional

seats in the quarter, resulting in INR2.38b of capitalization. We also invested INR1.06b in technology infrastructure and plan to end the year at INR14.88b in terms of capital expenditure. We made a payment of INR25.02b towards -- that is equivalent to $514.81m - towards the purchase of Citigroup Global Services Ltd, which has been renamed as TCS e-Serve. This (inaudible) transaction was concluded on December 31. Therefore, there was no effect on P&L as a result of this acquisition. However, the balance sheet contains the consolidated picture. I have talked about the currency movement. Our policy of hedging both receivables and revenues has proved to be prudent. We have taken hedges at the beginning of this fiscal to protect our revenue, since rupee was expected to appreciate. During the volatile movement in Q2, we have added to the hedges. Since rupee was in a depreciative state against the US dollar this quarter, we recorded a loss of INR2.03b in revenue hedging. However, I want to point out that we realized on US dollar -- after accounting for these hedging losses, the post-hedge realized rate was [INR46.75], which are higher than the previous quarter's post-hedge rate by 11%. Our policy of extending the hedging operations to protect receivables in other countries' currencies, such as pounds sterling, euro, South African rand, Swedish kroner and Australian dollar, ensured that we did not suffer major losses. Had we not covered that, we would have lost INR2.39b of -- if they had been left un-hedged. We did not take any additional revenue hedges in this quarter and are securing our position for Q4. With the economic environment being difficult, cash is certainly king. We made certain -- considerable improvement in our receivables picture, bringing it down by nine days. Even in respect of accounts which dissolved their businesses, our collections improved considerably. Even after the CGSL acquisition, we have available cash and fund investments of INR21.63b. Also during the quarter, we moved a considerable part of our funds to fixed deposits with Indian and foreign banks of proven rating, the auditors have physically verified their

funds deployment position. In closing, I would like to recap we have held course in very choppy waters and delivered growth. In difficult times like these, our focus has to be on managing risk, being disciplined and delivering profitable margins. We expect to continue on this path of operational efficiencies going forward as we build a robust Company for the future. Thank you. KEDAR SHIRALI: Thank you, Maha. Rochelle, we can now open the lines for questioning. OPERATOR: Thank you very much, Mr. Shirali. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin the question and answer session. (Operator Instructions). Our first question is from the line of Mr. Joseph Foresi of Janney Montgomery Scott. Please go ahead. JOSEPH FORESI, ANALYST, JANNEY MONTGOMERY SCOTT: Hi. Just a couple of quick questions here. First, on the Citigroup acquisition. In light of some of the news that's come out on the Company in these last couple of days, I wonder if you can give us an update on how you view that acquisition and some of its components and how the overall relationship is doing for you guys. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: The Citigroup relationship is doing overall very well. And if you look at the revenue streams for us, so far it has been on the technology side and now it will also be on the BPO side. And the news of the last couple of days does not impact us in terms of the revenue flows, so we don't think that that's going to have an impact on our revenue flows, on the current committed volume of business, both on the technology side and on the BPO side. So we expect to meet the plan numbers on the Citigroup side. We have spoken to them, not in the last couple of days, but over the last -- over the last quarter several times. And that's all I have to report. JOSEPH FORESI: And then, just on the pricing front, pricing came in, I'm assuming that it's probably due to currency this quarter, but we've heard stuff from competitors that the pricing environment's very difficult

from the -- coming both from the competitors and from the present client base. In your internal modeling, what have you put in for pricing going forward? Are you starting to see a more difficult environment? And maybe an order of magnitude, if you are? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: The pricing this quarter is -- has been flat, more or less. It's a 10 basis point drop on a constant currency basis. So I think, as I said in the opening remarks, we earlier in the quarter decided that we'll be very, very disciplined on the pricing, not that we were not before, but we thought that we've got to be more focused and it needed all the rigor. That's what we have executed and we think that we need to maintain that kind of rigor on managing and maintaining the pricing. Given the market environment, I must tell you that the pricing pressure is continuing and it's going to be there. So it is possible that the pricing may decline, but I won't be able to give you a definitive number. But all I would say is that we will continue to make our efforts to be very disciplined in the way we qualify the deals and do the pricing. JOSEPH FORESI: And will that pricing decline, if it does take place, show up next quarter, or is there a lag time between it? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Possibly there is a lag time. There is a lag time. But having said that -- having said that, normally, a year ago or even six quarters ago, if you had asked, I would have always said that what happens is -- in this quarter will not impact the next quarter. But the way that things are currently and the number of incidents we have seen in a quarter of 90 days, I think it's very, very, very volatile. So we'll be managing it daily basis, weekly basis. Very difficult to say. JOSEPH FORESI: And my last question here is just on the hiring environment. Maybe you could talk about how many offers you've put

out for next year, what you're currently doing on that front and if you've changed any of your hiring plans in the last two or three months. AJOY MUKHERJEE: Yes. As far as hiring is concerned, in this particular quarter, that is the quarter that we have just closed, the gross addition has been 11,773 and we have -- that takes us, as far as the financial year is concerned, 30,430 that we have already added. And for the next financial year, that is FY '10, the trainee offers that we have made is 24,800 plus. JOSEPH FORESI: And have you changed your hiring plans at all in the last three months? AJOY MUKHERJEE: As -- in this particular financial year, we said 30,000 to 35,000 and we are on track for 30,000 to 35,000. We already -- we have taken over 30,000. We have done 30,400-plus already. JOSEPH FORESI: Sure. I meant going forward. AJOY MUKHERJEE: Going forward, as -- as we are looking at the situation and the kind of business planning that we will be doing, we have done that we decide as to the joining plan and how exactly we will do the complete hiring. It's very difficult to give you a projection at this point in time. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I would just like to add to what Ajoy said. With regard to the lateral hires, definitely we have scaled down and we are watching the market ramp-up situation very carefully. And we will make a call again in February and in March. But lateral hires, we have definitely reduced drastically. JOSEPH FORESI: Okay. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Foresi. The next question is from the line of Mitali Ghosh of Merrill Lynch. Please go ahead. MITALI GHOSH, ANALYST, MERRILL LYNCH: Hi, good evening. I was just trying to reconcile the margin breakdown in terms of deconstructing the margin movement during the quarter, because with the rupee depreciating as well as the SG&A improvement that you have had, just wondering what -- how much the lower productivity actually contributed. So Maha, it would help a

lot if you could just deconstruct that for us, please. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Okay. The exchange gain was about 136 basis points. And offshore leverage about 25 basis points. And the SG&A improvement is about 166 basis points. And then, productivity, as well as some capacity creation in some of our global development centers, contributed to the extent of about 269 basis points negatively. So the sum total is 53% is the net improvement. S. MAHALINGAM: 53 basis -- N. CHANDRASEKARAN: 53 basis points is the net improvement. MITALI GHOSH: Right. So just as a follow-up to that, in terms of when you say productivity -- lower productivity, how does that tie in with the 10 basis points that you mentioned from a pricing perspective? And if you could just clarify again whether that 10 basis points is the change in blended US dollar rate or is that in constant currency that we're talking? UNIDENTIFIED COMPANY REPRESENTATIVE: You know, Mitali -- N. CHANDRASEKARAN: That is in constant currency. UNIDENTIFIED COMPANY REPRESENTATIVE: Yes. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: The 10 basis points is in constant currency. The other break-up I gave you on the exchange and the offshore movement and the 269 basis points negatively also involves some capacity creation we made in some of our development centers for specific engagements, project-related. MITALI GHOSH: Okay. And just on the environment, if you can help us understand that, in the last couple of months, what is the customer behavior you're seeing? This is typically the time, I guess, that people at least start thinking about budgets. I know things are not frozen yet, but what is the kind of customer conversations you've been having on maybe project ramp-ups, what they're thinking of spending? Are they actually going to be breaking up the budget and maybe not giving you an indication for the full year, but just for the next couple of quarters?. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: It's a mixed bag. It's a mixed bag, Mitali. There are some clients who have finalized the budget and we have a pretty good indication of what we are going to do

with them. There are other clients who have not finalized the budget and will -- clarity will emerge as we go into the quarter. And I think, because of the uncertainty that we are experiencing, we should expect surprises. Surprises may come in the form of -- like what happened to Nortel, or it may happen in the form of some clients cancelling projects. So that kind of negative surprises, we should anticipate and we should factor in when we see -- when we have our growth plans. On the pricing, as I said, so far, we have been able to maintain the pricing. But the pressure will be there and it is likely that there can be dips. And in terms of the sectors, I think retail, utilities, pharma are doing much better compared to BFS, manufacturing, telecom and high-tech. That's the indication. And you know, while the US geography is the most watched geography, I would say that, out of the six deals we won, large deals we announced today, five of them came from the US geography. So that is the kind of -- may I say a contradiction. So opportunities are there. At the same time, you should expect surprises. MITALI GHOSH: Thanks. And just finally, in terms of the -- in the context of the margin outlook, what should we expect for this year? And then, next year, if -- given the uncertain outlook, in terms of campus offers made, how would you really look at maybe deferring rates or -- how would you look at managing utilization which actually seemed to drop this quarter? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Maybe on utilization I would say that we have dropped, because it was expected and it's also reflected in the volume, I mean. And we -- I think it will go back up again. Already, we are seeing slight improvements in utilization in the early January. Again, we have won and announced quite a number of deals. It all depends on whether all of them will ramp up as per plan or there will be delays. If the

ramp-ups happen and the customers put focus to aggressively ramp up, then the utilization can come up. Otherwise, we've got to watch this carefully. As I already said that, on the recruitment side, we have gone very slow on the laterals, lateral hires. And also, we are driving more offshore movement. We already moved this quarter about 160 basis points, which is on top of a significant movement we did last quarter. And we expect to continue the push and you will see offshore movements in the coming quarters. The trainee hires for the next year, yes, you know how many offers we have made next year. Ajoy already shared it. But the whole joining, etc., I think we'll think the overall situation based on the demand sometime in February. MITALI GHOSH: Okay. Thank you very much. OPERATOR: Thank you, Miss Ghosh. The next question is from the line of Mr. Moshe Katri of Cowen and Company. Please go ahead. MOSHE KATRI, ANALYST, COWEN AND COMPANY: Hey, thanks. Nice quarter, guys. Looking at your pipeline and if we try to compare it to the previous quarter, can you kind of give us a feel by trend? Is it up, down, flat? Can you also comment on sales cycles? Is -- are they longer or shorter or similar? I guess we're trying to understand whether things have changed much since the September quarter. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I think -- if you recall, the September quarter and the June quarter, one thing we said about the environment is very client-specific. We kept repeating that it is very client-specific. But now, we would say that, apart from being the client-specific situations -- and definitely we are seeing slowdown in manufacturing, high-tech and telecom, as I articulated. Now, with regard to the deal pipeline, the deal pipeline per se is healthy. We have announced six deals and some of them are very sizeable deals. And the number of deals we are pursuing is quite healthy and it is distributed across geography. We have a good number of deals going on in UK, Europe, Asia Pacific,

as well as in other parts of the world. But the concern is sometimes the deals take longer than before. And the second concern is whether the ramp-ups will happen as per plan. Previously, I would say that we were very, very certain about the ramp-ups. Now, we worry about the -- about the ramp-ups. That's the only extra comment and caution that I would like to add. MOSHE KATRI: Okay. And then, what sort of projects are being funded these days, looking at the pipeline? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Yes, I think there are different kinds of projects. The two large ones I announced are full services deals, transformation deals where we take over the complete application portfolio, infrastructure portfolio and the business operations in both the situations. And then, also, implementing a major transformation program. In the case of the retail company, it is regarding optimization of inventory and those kind of transformation programs. In the case of the large manufacturer, we won another deal this quarter which is a global implementation of ERP across several countries. So there are deals driven by enterprise solutions, SAP and Oracle implementations in multi-country implementations, consolidation (inaudible) definitely, that -- those type of deals are coming. And full services deals, as well as vendor consolidation and [cost off] deals. The financial services deal that we announced this quarter is a vendor consolidation, where the company is migrating -- is consolidating everything to us and application portfolio and offshoring significantly. So these are the three trends, I would say. MOSHE KATRI: Great. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Katri. The next question is from the line of Divya Nagarajan of JM Financial. Please go ahead. DIVYA NAGARAJAN, ANALYST, JM FINANCIAL: Hi, congrats on the quarter. I just wanted to know, of the deals that you've signed this quarter, what were the kind of -- what is the nature of the deals and how are they different from the large deals that you've been signing in the earlier quarters? Yes, hi. In case you didn't get my question earlier, I -- my question was with

reference to the large deals you've signed and if they are any different from the nature of the deals, large deals, that you have been signing in earlier quarters. And secondly, could you also give us a sense of how many of your top 10 or 20 clients would currently be consolidating vendors, please? S. RAMADORAI: On the first question I think no. There are -- if you are asking about the business model there is no change in the business model. There is no change in the structuring of the deal or anything. It is pretty much similar to the kind of large deals we did before. And these deals are either offshoring deals or offshoring of IT infrastructure and BPO, those kinds of full services deals. Then with regard to the second question I really can't answer this question. I think if you really see our results this quarter we have dropped in the use of the top client. But otherwise if you see the top five and top 10 and all that I think we have managed to keep the revenues in line with the Company growth rate, we have not dropped revenues. So I think it's quite healthy. DIVYA NAGARAJAN: Just one more question, you spoke about 1.2% growth in constant currency terms. Could you split it into your volume and pricing impact in that, please? S. MAHALINGAM: You should take it as pretty much volume. It is because we said you see the 2 point or 2% is the volume in rupee terms, and the pricing is pretty much flat. So I would just say that that 1.23% you should take it as that. DIVYA NAGARAJAN: And how would you reconcile this with the 250 for -- 242 bps volume growth that you were talking about earlier? S. MAHALINGAM: The offshoring was down by [106] basis points, and then the pricing drops by 10 basis points. DIVYA NAGARAJAN: Thanks. All the best. OPERATOR: Thank you, Miss Nagarajan. The next question is from the line of Mr. [Sandeep Motangi] of [IIFO] please go ahead. SANDEEP MOTANGI,

ANALYST, IIFO: Yes hi, Chandra, it's a good quarter. I have two questions, the first one is on pricing, despite the really challenging environment on pricing so far you seen to be able to evade the pricing declines. Can you just elaborate on what kind of -- what is the extent of pricing cuts that clients have been demanding? And so far what is the value proposition of the offshore mix that you guys have been suggesting to the clients to evade the pricing? S. MAHALINGAM: [Shirali], evading the pricing. Yes, I think clearly pricing pressure can always be there even in a very good quarter, even in a very good environment pricing pressure can always be there. I think what is happening is that if you really look at it customers are looking at a certain amount of efficiencies that they want to bring in, so depending upon the specific situation in each client, especially when we are there in those clients for long periods of time. We are getting our teams to sit down and go through what has been the value proposition. One value proposition that has been pretty consistent with all our clients is our experience certainty in terms of our delivery. And to some extent this helps us also because in the uncertain times the last thing that clients want is more delivery problems. And which will again result in additional work, re-work and so on so forth. And apart from that all the other operating parameters we are looking at, and all the other consolidation opportunities, not only offshoring opportunities, re-platforming opportunities, we look at across the board what all we can do, including what we call the technology consultant management and then carve out a unique value proposition for each client. So it's very difficult for me just to say that this value proposition is applicable to all clients. It does require knowledge of the customer, knowledge of the systems. And, of course, the track record which the client respects, so all of. And then finally you've got to deliver what the client

want. At the end of the day in productivity you have got to deliver, that's also very important. So I think a combination of factors, and we have been disciplined about doing it. SANDEEP MOTANGI: Yes, thanks for this. And just one thing, could you clarify on the extent of revenue exposure to Nortel? S. MAHALINGAM: Nortel, on a quarterly basis, I would just say that it's about -- in the region of about $5m, $6m. SANDEEP MOTANGI: Okay, thanks. That's all. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Motangi. The next question is from the line of Mr. Julio Quinteros of Goldman Sachs please go ahead. JULIO QUINTEROS, ANALYST, GOLDMAN SACHS: Great, thanks, S. Just wanted to go back to a quick comment on the -- I guess I am trying to reconcile more than anything else is your commentary that you are not seeing cancellations. There appear to be some delays, but yet the deceleration in growth that we are seeing is still represented in the numbers that you guys are reporting. So, when you are slowing down the way that you are and the way that the business is kind of trending right now if it's not cancellation or delay driven what actually is leading to the slowdowns that you guys are seeing in the model? S. RAMADORAI: Well, I am sorry I don't think I ever said we are not seeing cancellations. I clearly said we are seeing slowdown and cancellations, and I also named the sectors, apart from BFS, it's manufacturing, telecom, hi-tech and transportation. And these are the sectors in which we are seeing the slowdown. We experienced cancellations. We experienced what we call it, some clients really even in T&M contracts, cancelled some projects. So these are the sectors and it is happening. And -- but there are other sectors, which we saw growing. But again, I still maintain that regard to desegregate the data by client things are happening client specific. Overall there is some [affinity] towards some sectors. JULIO QUINTEROS: Okay. And then just related to that can you distinguish between application outsourcing work

versus development work? So is it -- the project cancellation is more development work versus the outsourcing work. In other words, is the outsourcing work continuing to sort of run on its course. S. RAMADORAI: I think you are right, you are right with your assessment on that. JULIO QUINTEROS: Okay, great. Thanks, S. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Quinteros. Our next question is from the line of Mr. Sandeep Shah of ICICI Securities. SANDEEP SHAH, ANALYST, ICICI SECURITIES: Yes, just wanted to ask in terms of the various contracts which are outstanding in terms of forwards for the coming quarter as well as FY'10 and beyond. S. MAHALINGAM: So there is no change from the figures that I have given in the last quarter. As I said we have not added to the hedges except to the extent of about $250m that we took in this quarter. We have not cancelled anything in terms of futures. So it's -- whatever we have said earlier continues. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay. So the [OCL] position has changed on a quarter-on-quarter basis. S. MAHALINGAM: The OCL position has changed. At this moment in time it is INR7.5b. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay, thanks. KEDAR SHIRALI: Next question, Rochelle. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Shah. The next question is from the line of Mr. Anthony Miller of TechMarketView. Please go ahead. ANTHONY MILLER, ANALYST, TECHMARKETVIEW: Yes, hello, gentlemen. I've got one question and a couple of points of clarification. Firstly, on Satyam, can you just give us some idea please of home many -- what proportion of say your top 20 customers are shared with Satyam, and what reaction you're seeing from those customers? Are they actively coming to you now and asking you to take over their work? S. MAHALINGAM: First, before I answer your question I want to make a small correction on the previous question. A gentleman asked me about our revenues, quarterly revenues on Nortel, it's a little under $10m. It's closer to $10m per quarter, so I wanted to make this correction. Then moving on I think in -- I can't give you

the exact number of clients that we are overlapping with another company. I think with many companies our clients overlap. But by and large, I would say that there are clients who have approached us to take over work and all that. Our guideline with which we have instructed our teams and how we operate is we are not proactively going after any of their clients. But when there are opportunities, if the deal makes sense, definitely, we will look at it. That's the approach we are taking. ANTHONY MILLER: Okay. And just to clarify a couple of things. Firstly, on European growth, you said that five of the six big deals you've announced were in North America, but you said the pipeline is pretty even across geographies. Now, it's clear from the numbers that European growth was much slower, in fact it had declined more so than North America. Why is it? Is it the decisions in Europe are taking longer or is it the pipeline is declining faster? S. MAHALINGAM: No, actually you are looking at the number based on the currency this quarter. You had a currency -- rupee appreciation against the pound and euro. So given the situation here, look at constant currency, in constant currency terms we did extremely well in Europe. In fact, we had a sequential growth of 380 basis points in the UK and 410 basis points in Europe this quarter. So Europe and UK have done extremely well this quarter in terms of sequential growth. Now, the deal pipeline when I said that five deals of the large -- the six deals we announced coming from the US there are no revenues of those deals reflected in this quarter. That will come in the quarters to follow. ANTHONY MILLER: And just finally a point of clarification on the budgets. You said you have some clients had fixed their budgets. Of those that have fixed their budgets, where is the direction of those budgets? Where are they spending more? And where are they spending less? S. MAHALINGAM: I think the clients who

have fixed their budgets are two kinds. There are clients where the companies are doing well and then they are fully going ahead with their developmental projects as well as maintenance projects. So there they are spending both on maintenance and transformation. There are other clients who are only focused primarily on [cost off] where in those situations there are no transformational or developmental projects. The whole thing is about cost off. So these are the two types we are seeing, very clear category of clients. And there is a third set of clients who are still working on their plans, and we still don't have visibility yet. ANTHONY MILLER: Okay. Thanks very much indeed. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Miller. The next question is from the line of Mr. Vikas Jadhav of Motilal Oswal Securities please go ahead. VIKAS JADHAV, ANALYST, MOTILAL OSWAL SECURITIES: Yes, hi. My question was on the (inaudible), although you have done a very good job on cross-rationalization from all the heads like (inaudible) and all. But there was a lot of [under-reconciled] on the employee cost part that has actually slightly declined. S. RAMADORAI: Employee cost has declined in -- because in the SG&A is down, but if we are really looking at the combination of the [OR] SG&A have gone up. VIKAS JADHAV: Okay. And secondly, India business actually has been [growing] for the last two quarters so that was a bit of a surprise. S. MAHALINGAM: India business we grew this quarter, grew last quarter. Q1 was a decline, Q2 was a growth, Q3 is a decline. It is one area we are looking at because India business traditionally has been very volatile. And sometimes it so happens that in a quarter where the rest of the world are not growing the India clients that affects the performance. So it does happen, primarily because most of the programs in India, as you know, is all developmental and transformational programs. They are not entity contracts. So we are really looking at it to see what we can do to reduce the volatility in India.

VIHANG NAIK, ANALYST, MOTILAL OSWAL SECURITIES: Yes, hi this is Vihang. I have a question, we mentioned that exposure to Nortel at around $10m per quarter, is there any outstanding receivables we have right now? S. MAHALINGAM: Yes. We -- so far -- I'll say a couple of things. One is that the payment with Nortel has been on time all through. We've had a relationship with Nortel for more than 20 years. It's been a very long standing relationship. And, in fact, I got calls today from them saying that this -- they are continuing to -- there are plans are to continuing to do work. So we have to wait, they told us they will give us more color and more insights as we go into the next few days. In terms of outstandings, it is a few million dollars, [Phi]? PHIROZ VANDREVALA: Yes, few million dollars. S. RAMADORAI: No. I'll check and come back to you on that. VIKAS JADHAV: Sure, okay. Thanks that's all from my side. OPERATOR: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Samad Masood of Ovum. Please go ahead. SAMAD MASOOD, ANALYST, OVUM: Hello, guys. Thanks for taking my question. I have -- just wanted to get a bit more detail on the vertical performance. You mentioned that manufacturing, telecoms and high-tech had been affected quite badly. But just looking at a quick analysis of your results, it seems that your manufacturing business has actually grown by 16% in this quarter. And I was wondering how does that tally with the fact that you are saying that you are actually seeing a slowdown in manufacturing? And I'd also like to ask also about -- we had a question earlier about application development, and that that's sort of ticking along not growing spectacularly. But I see there is actually quite a lot of growth in your engineering and industrial and infrastructure services. And I was wondering if you could also provide a bit more detail behind that, seeing as they are the only two areas that seem to be growing significantly

right now. S. MAHALINGAM: I think the manufacturing side -- I don't know where you look at it, but the -- in terms of constant currency we have a drop of 220 basis points in manufacturing in this quarter over the previous quarter. And also, when we say that we are seeing some slowdown we take into account not only the current quarter performance, we take into account deal closes, not only the deal pipeline the deal closes and the customers affinity to doing development projects and transformation projects. So we do quite a bit of analysis, and based on this I have to tell you that we will expect slowdown in this sector at least in the immediate quarters. Then in terms of the second question, I think the services side you are right. We are doing quite well in terms of the application development. It is growing nicely. And also our full services deals are gaining a lot of traction. So infrastructure and BPO along with application development as an integrated offering is a very important portfolio that we have, and that is getting a lot of traction. And we also mentioned in our commentary as part of the deck that the infrastructure services is poised to grow as customers unbundle their contracts. SAMAD MASOOD: Okay, thank you. That's all I wanted to know. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Masood. The next question is from the line of Mr. Julio Quinteros of Goldman Sachs please go ahead. JULIO QUINTEROS: I just wanted to follow up on your comments about the Citi situation. It sounded like you guys have not had any recent conversations. When you guys signed this contract back in December when the deal was closed what were the terms at that point in time? In other words, with the breakup potential here are you guys really still expecting the same volume trends or that none of that would actually change based on what you guys were expecting when you originally signed the contract? S. RAMADORAI: Yes, after December 31 I think we have had a conversation. Based

on this breakup we don't see any drop in volume coming to us. JULIO QUINTEROS: Was it factored into your original expectations that they would actually break up Citibank? S. RAMADORAI: See the -- if you ask me whether they will break up that -- this particular unit, I mean we didn't factor that and that's the negotiation we have. The contract that today we have is with the Citigroup and the business that we are doing is not part of SSB, it's in the other areas. JULIO QUINTEROS: Okay, got it. Okay, got it. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Quinteros. The next question is from the line of Nitin Padmanabhan of Centrum Broking. Please go ahead. NITIN PADMANABHAN, ANALYST, CENTRUM BROKING: Yes hi. I was just looking at the overall headcount that you've added this time 8,000 and odd. It's, I think, more of trainees. So, are we likely to see -- these would have been committed -- so, going forward into next quarter are we likely to see a similar number? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: No going forward -- see if you look at our total trainee count that we have added, given our -- also what we have done last year, we have done between -- close to 19,800 trainees that we have added in this three quarters. Next quarter the number of trainees, that we have given, most of them have come in. So as a result -- of course, there will be some trainees who are left that they will join. And lateral hires as we have told you earlier, experience says that we have -- controlling it very tightly and that we have reduced significantly. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Okay. This -- that I couldn't reconcile laterals. You look at it this quarter we did 1,696. If you look at it last quarter we did 1,587. So actually there was an increase in laterals. So I was wondering when our utilization is under pressure, I think we are seeing some pressure within the top clients. So, why are lateral intakes so high at this point in time?

N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Yes, I think, the major part of the lateral hires you see this quarter of 1,600 odd, more than 1,100, I think close to 1,200 of that is predominantly in Latin America. And it is a combination of there we don't distinguish between the trainees and laterals as we are building up to business. That's the pool that we have created there because of the local talent and the contract that's required. And the remaining 450 or 500 people that you are seeing here, some of them are the offers that were close towards the end of the last quarter and we have taken them on board in various specialist skills, especially areas like SAP, Oracle applications and so on and so forth. And since then I think we are controlling the lateral hires, so that's the (inaudible). NITIN PADMANABHAN: All right. And within the top clients I think there has been some pressure there. So is that something that is likely to continue going forward? And in terms of the total client mix that we have in terms of $1m, 20,000, 30,000, there again have we seen a churn, have we seen some sort of something going out and something coming in, although it looks stagnant on the higher end of it. Has that happened? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: No, I think we have done well on the clients. But if you really look at it when you see a higher [NV] the 100m but if you look at the 15m and below 20m we have nicely migrated customers upwards. We've added to 50m clients, we've added four clients to 20m plus. So it's nicely migrating up even at the 10m rate. But having said that the top client has showed some de-growth to this quarter. And you know in our large pool of top 10, 15, 20 clients, even in a very good market you could expect that there will be some clients who will do -- grow well in one quarter and other clients will drop the quarter. That kind of volatility you should expect. And definitely

you should expect it in an environment which is so tough. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Right. And just two more, one is that if you look at for the next year the kind of offers that we have given for freshers, and looking into the kind of pressure that is building up in terms of utilization at this point, is it more so -- or is it that we will be able to maintain utilization at these levels or we will see it dropping, keeping the current environment in mind? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: What is your second question you can complete that, and then I'll answer both. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Yes. The second one is that -- no, I think you can go ahead with the -- I'll get back. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Okay. On the -- we already answered (inaudible). Our intent is to maintain utilization. We are used to maintaining the utilization between 76% and 78% until a few quarters back. But about two quarters back we said that we are going to push it to 80%, 81% and we did that last quarter. It has come down to 79.9% it's not a bad utilization at all. It's a pretty healthy utilization. In fact, we can I hope, even bring it down by another couple of more points in general. To maintain between the 77% to 80% is a very good healthy utilization is what we feel. But our endeavor is to push the utilization up. And as we articulated before we will take a quarter to [do it]. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Okay. And just one last -- KEDAR SHIRALI: We are running out of time. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Yes. KEDAR SHIRALI: So I will now request Mr. Ramadorai to make his closing remarks. S. RAMADORAI: Thank you, everyone. What I wanted to say was we are living in times of volatility, and this is across sectors and across geographies. The focus should be and will be vis-a-vis TCS on operational efficiencies and delivering a value proposition. There are going to be pricing pressures, and how you articulate and how you stand up to it

and how you position yourself has to be seen. From a volatility of foreign exchange point of view again, the rupee versus the dollar, the dollar versus the pound or the euro are all behaving pretty volatile conditions there. The strategic teams are building for the future in terms of multi-geography business models as well as focusing on the domestic market will continue to be there for us, so widespread across geographies and across verticals. We are likely to experience delays in wrap-ups as well as in decision making. And all of our focus on building for the future will be around building efficiencies and looking at the future, and investing for the future on people and some of the assets which we create, while focusing on the clients and enabling value delivery. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, sir. Thank you, gentlemen, of the Management. Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of TCS that concludes this evening's conference call. Thank you for joining us and you may now disconnect your lines. Thank you. Full text: OPERATOR: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. I am Prateba, the moderator for this conference. Welcome to the TCS conference call. For the duration of the presentation all participants' lines will be in the listen-only mode. The presentation will be followed by a question and answer session conducted first for participants at the international bridge, followed by a Q&A session for participants at India. I would now like to hand over to Mr. David Nelson. Thank you and over to you, sir. DAVID NELSON, HEAD OF GLOBAL IR, TCS: Good evening. Welcome everyone and thank you for joining us on the TCS earnings call for quarter 3, FY 2007. I'm David Nelson, Head of Global Investor Relations. Please note that this call is being webcast through our website and an archive, including transcript, will be available on the site for the duration of the quarter. The financial statements results presentation and press release are also available on our website. Our leadership team is present on this call to discuss our results. We have with us Mr. S. Ramadorai, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director. S. RAMADORAI, CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER AND MANAGING DIRECTOR, TCS: Good evening, good morning, to everyone. DAVID NELSON: We also have with us Maha, who is our Chief Financial Officer. S. MAHALINGHAM, CFO, TCS: Good evening, good morning. DAVID NELSON: We also have our three Executive Vice-Presidents. Chandra, who is Head of Global Sales and Operations. N. CHANDRASEKARAN, HEAD OF GLOBAL SALES AND OPERATIONS, TCS: Hello, good morning and good afternoon, and good evening. up. We are doing a good number of projects, $10m plus, $15m plus etc., and those projects lend themselves for us to show our efficiency superiority. CHANDRASEKARAN: I don't think so, primarily, because if those contracts had brought down the billing rate numbers, you would have seen it in the margins and that did not happen. And every time there is [the effect of] margins it's something that we will explain and [inaudible]. SEKHAR SINGH: Yes. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Yes, FNS it's a fantastic product. This [inaudible] deal and the [China] deal that we talked about, definitely the only product that could meet the benchmark. The benchmarking we had to do was to be able to support 360m accounts and that's the kind of benchmarking that we're able to demonstrate. Apparently [inaudible] over the last 12 months very significantly in terms of upgrading the technologies [inaudible] architecture. In terms of our functionality tests they are the finest functionalities in terms of core banking. That, coupled with all the wholesale banking assets that we have and the insurance [assets] we have, we probably have one of the strongest footprints in terms of a financial services solution contract. PADMANABHAN: Sekhar, we normally don't give the break-up of the staff -- SEKHAR SINGH: Last time, it was actually mentioned in the analysts' presentation. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: We'll give it to you later [inaudible] handy right now. SEKHAR SINGH: Thanks. Goodbye. OPERATOR: Thank you very much, sir. BREA ROMEDA: Sure, thanks very much. Just as a [data] point, if you could finally give us a flavor on [inaudible] progress [inaudible] margins for the current quarter, actually? S. Full text: OPERATOR: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. I am Prateba, the moderator for this conference. Welcome to the TCS conference call. For the duration of the presentation all participants' lines will be in the listen-only mode. The presentation will be followed by a question and answer session conducted first for participants at the international bridge, followed by a Q&A session for participants at India. I would now like to hand over to Mr. David Nelson. Thank you and over to you, sir. DAVID NELSON, HEAD OF GLOBAL IR, TCS: Good evening. Welcome everyone and thank you for joining us on the TCS earnings call for quarter 3, FY 2007. I'm David Nelson, Head of Global Investor Relations. Please note that this call is being webcast through our website and an archive, including transcript, will be available on the site for the duration of the quarter. The financial statements results presentation and press release are also available on our website. Our leadership team is present on this call to discuss our results. We have with us Mr. S. Ramadorai, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director. S. RAMADORAI, CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER AND MANAGING DIRECTOR, TCS: Good evening, good morning, to everyone. DAVID NELSON: We also have with us Maha, who is our Chief Financial Officer. S. MAHALINGHAM, CFO, TCS: Good evening, good morning. DAVID NELSON: We also have our three Executive Vice-Presidents. Chandra, who is Head of Global Sales and Operations. N. CHANDRASEKARAN, HEAD OF GLOBAL SALES AND OPERATIONS, TCS: Hello, good morning and good afternoon, and good evening. DAVID NELSON: We have with us Paddy, Head of Global Human Resources. S. PADMANABHAN, HEAD OF GLOBAL HUMAN RESOURCES, TCS: Hello, everyone. DAVID NELSON: And Phiroz, Head of Global Corporate Affairs. PHIROZ VANDREVALA, HEAD OF GLOBAL CORPORATE AFFAIRS, TCS: Hi, everyone. DAVID NELSON: Mr. Ramadorai and Mr. Mahalingham will begin with a brief overview of the Company's performance followed by the Q&A session. As you are aware, TCS does not provide specific revenue and earnings guidance. Furthermore,

anything said on this call which reflects our outlook for the future, or which can be construed as a forward-looking statement, must be viewed in conjunction with the risks that the Company faces. These risks are outlined on the second slide of our results presentation. With that, I'll turn the call over to Mr. Ramadorai to begin the proceedings. S. RAMADORAI: Thank you so much, and we have had an exceptionally good quarter 3. And in the nine months we crossed in terms of revenue $3b. And we have had the distinction of earning $1b in revenue in a single quarter. The quarter 3 revenue is more than $1b. We have also reached a mark in terms of $250m in terms of net profits during this quarter 3. The momentum, going forward, we have it very good with a healthy build up of clients. In terms of operational excellence we have demonstrated our global network delivery model where delivery happens in addition to India out of the customer locations as well as our global delivery centers. We won some major deals this quarter. One of the major ones was a deal from Latin America, where one of Ecuador's largest banks has engaged TCS for an integrated asset plus BPO and IT services worth more than $140m. This essentially showcases the strategy taken in new markets and also an integrated full services play. The large engagements are extremely important to us. They are not only profitable, but also provide the room to increase our share of the wallet through value-added services and delivery excellence. All along we have been saying that we will certainly focus and look at large deals in addition to the others, and they give us sustained profitable revenue as well as potential opportunities for leveraging all the offerings as an integrated full services provider, and a global network delivery model in terms of delivering an operational excellence being the key. Our CFO, Mr. Mahalingham, will explain both in terms of revenue growth, volume growth, price increases, better business mix, offshore leverage and how we have addressed all

of this. And Chandra, heading our global operations and sales, will touch upon the whole momentum with regard to the type of business geography-wise, service-wise, as well as industry-wise. We added 24,000 professionals so far and expect to reach 30,000 plus professionals by the end of this financial year. The attrition, which is one of the parameters which we look at, however you slice the dice the numbers of attrition, has been the lowest in the industry. And our retention has been exceptionally good based on how we [billed] our people and how we retain them. So let me wish you all a very happy 2007 and beyond, and hand over to Mr. Mahalingham, our Chief Financial Officer. S. MAHALINGHAM: Thank you, Ram. As we have stated previously, we are not just gunning for growth, but sustained, profitable growth, and we have delivered it again in Q3. As you can see, our overall total revenue increased 8.4% quarter-on-quarter and 14.8% year-on-year in rupee terms. This is against a backdrop of appreciating rupee. It shows not only our strong operational performance, but also the robust financial management that we have put in play. Strong demands from our clients, as we have seen through strong sequential year-over-year revenue growth via data integrated services strategy, delivered through our Global Network Delivery model. When you look at our financial performance we have had consecutive quarters of margin improvement, and our cost management program, coupled with growth of [delivering] reserves. We have also put programs in place to optimize our operations and thereby ensure that our financial objectives for the year are being met. Now I'd like to walk you through two key points after which we'll open up for questions. The first one is about the strong demand for our portfolio services globally. The underlying strength of TCS's business model is illustrated by a strong revenue growth. If you look at it in overall U.S. dollar terms, our revenue has grown to $1.098b in Q3, from $975.43m in Q2; a sequential growth of 12.6%. This strong revenue growth was fuelled by volume growth, as

Ram said, by better business mix but I think from improved resource allocation as we moved the value chain, as well as, of course, better pricing. I'm sure I'm going to get a lot of questions on this, so I want to detail out the revenue growth story for all of you. Volume has grown by 7.87% in this quarter. Billing rate on [some] material contracts has given us a 2% growth. Pricing plus [productivity] combined on turnkey projects has given us 2.59% growth. Exchange has actually come down -- has resulted in revenues being recognized at a lower rate to the extent of 2.46%. Offshore shift, which I'm sure all of you know is pretty good for margin, but certainly from a revenue perspective the revenue comes down, that has accounted for a reduction in revenue to the extent of 1.56% and, therefore, the total is 8.44%. Having dealt with the revenue story, let me deal with the margin story. As I have said we have set the platforms in place to ensure sustained improvement [in margin]. Our operating margin moved up 79 basis points to [26.08] from [25.29%] in Q2 this year. And this was being driven by higher pricing, improved productivity and a continued shift of work offshore. And, of course, when you take the model that many of you adopted on our improvement quarter, many of you said that foreign exchange, again, that we have needed to be removed from the sustainability margin. So if I moved equally the depreciation that we have had, our operating margin would have been higher by 1.37% out of approximately 27.45% in total for operating margin. Last, but not the least, in Q2 we talked about leveraging our cost base to drive an improvement in operating margins. We have made further progress in this direction. SG&A, as a percentage of revenue, as you can see, is climbing by 69 basis points to 19.4%. We, of course, had indicated a slightly lower figure as our goal so you can continue to expect some further improvements in this area. But to recap

the [conservance] of our margin improvement will be as follows; pricing 1.74%, that contributed 1.74% for our margin, cost efficiency, 0.14%. The reason I'm saying 0.14%, it is riding on what some of you considered as exceptional items last quarter. So I'm taking that also into account and it is 0.14%. Offshore shift 0.28%. ForEx has, in terms of our margins, declined by 1.37% and that's how we get our total figure of 79 basis points. As we can -- as you know this margin improvement has been achieved in spite of the one-off benefit recorded last quarter at [double to the expenses], 76 basis points. Regarding the full year we have stated our intention to maintain margins for the full year in the same ballpark as last year. As you can see, in spite of an appreciation in the rupee, we have continued to improve our margin. And we have continued to crank up the revenue and cost levers. And we have put in place programs to optimize our operation. And you have seen that direction that we have taken. Thank you. DAVID NELSON: We'll now open up the call for questions. OPERATOR: Thank you very much, sir. At this moment I would like to hand over the floor to Laurie to conduct the Q&A session for participants at the international bridge. This will be followed by a Q&A session for participants at India. Thank you, and over to Laurie. OPERATOR: Thank you, Prateba. We will now begin the Q&A session for participants connected to the WebEx international bridge. [OPERATOR INSTRUCTIONS]. Your first question comes from the line of Trip Chowdhry of Global Equities Research. TRIP CHOWDHRY, ANALYST, GLOBAL EQUITIES RESEARCH: Congratulations on a very solid quarter. A few questions here. First, I was wondering, for Chandra, regarding the sales execution, can you help us understand, from an operational perspective, what is the difference between winning a $50m plus deal and winning a $5m plus deal in terms of sale cycles, margins and ramp-up? Then I have a follow-up question. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Thank you. Fundamentally speaking, you can't generalize

CHANDRASEKARAN: Yes, I think, again, the infrastructure is an area which is having a tremendous uptake. Last quarter, we announced a $50m plus deal in infrastructure. This quarter, one of the $100m deals we have announced is in the infrastructure space, totally an infrastructure deal, more than $100m. It's a global deal [for this year] using our Global Network Delivery model and does not include any [asset take] or anything as part of that [inaudible] that I'm talking about. There is another infrastructure deal which we have won along with [ABM], the ABM and infrastructure together. That's the retail deal which

we announced $70m. Apart from that, our existing customers, who are large customers of ABM services, have [inaudible] infrastructure deals of the order of $20, $25m, so on and so forth. So in terms of infrastructure services, it's really attractive for us and a lot of [inaudible] customers and Q4 is going to be a ramp-up for infrastructure services business. BREA ROMEDA: Sure, thanks very much. Just as a [data] point, if you could finally give us a flavor on [inaudible] progress [inaudible] margins for the current quarter, actually? S. MAHALINGHAM: We are on the way to achieving the EBITDA margin, which is in the single digits, as part of this [inaudible]. Even in this current quarter we have had a positive operating margin. BREA ROMEDA: So, a single digit would mean in the middle range of 5 to 6%? S. MAHALINGHAM: [inaudible]. BREA ROMEDA: I'm just trying to get -- given that you already mentioned that the four-year process is [inaudible] a bit more -- S. BREA ROMEDA: Sure. S. RAMADORAI: As we combine both of them, we are certainly in the range of closer to the [10%]. BREA ROMEDA: Sure, and in terms of cross-selling on the same? RAMADORAI: And we are [well in line]. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: [Brea] infrastructure [inaudible] itself is a cross-sell deal. [inaudible] was a big [inaudible] customer [inaudible] for 20 years and then [we sold] the BPO. As part of the BPO, we are also doing infrastructure support. So there is a certain amount of offshoring of the infrastructure work that will happen in Q4 and

Q1 of the next financial year. So that [inaudible] operating improvement. So there are three different initiatives. One is the BPO, second is IT support in terms of infrastructure, third one is the transformation. All the three are happening and attracting [inaudible] to make improvements in margin but, as I said, the transformation is a program that is scheduled for four years. BREA ROMEDA: Sure. Thanks very much, and wish you all the best. OPERATOR: Thank you very much, madam. Participants are requested to kindly restrict to one question in the initial round. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I think if you really look at our portfolio, as you rightly pointed out, of the five deals we announced we announced them in five different continents, so there is a growth in every area of operation and every geography in which we operate. Some of our large customers trying to take advantage of the fact that we have such a high-quality center in these regions to offshore work to those locations. So the type of deal will vary. In addition to that, the emerging markets definitely are very attractive from the point of view of leveraging our assets, especially financial services product solutions. So you will see the trend of the

SAMEER GOYAL: Okay. Just wanted to have an update on what's happening on the new services clients like transportation, energy, even [inaudible] practices. It seems to be declining in terms of revenue for a couple of quarters. Any views on that? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Well, I think the travel and transportation business is not declining, it's -- what you are seeing is only completion of some fixed-price engagements. As you know, we already announced the Qantas deal this quarter, so the ramp-up is happening and you will see those things continuing to grow. Also, one of the things that we want to highlight is that the others -- I'm just trying to get the data, give me a minute. At the end, it will be [inaudible] come down, predominantly because there was some

major transformation programs that we did in the U.K. for one of the utility companies and that finished -- the [significant] finish was completed in the last quarter. There is some additional work that is coming up, but at this point in time in this quarter we did not get that [line growing], but it will grow again. So, both for transportation and energy and utilities, the [inaudible] is good and you will see them growing again. SAMEER GOYAL: So that significant jump what we saw in [life sciences] and retail this quarter. Was it due to some completion of projects in the [inaudible] practices also and we might see some decline happening in the coming quarters? N.
