Full text: OPERATOR: Ladies and gentlemen, good morning and good evening. I am Rochelle, the moderator for this conference call. Welcome to the TCS Earnings Conference Call. Please note that for the duration of this presentation, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and this conference is being recorded. After the presentation there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions. (OPERATOR INSTRUCTIONS). At this time I would like to turn the conference over to Mr. David Nelson, Head of Global Investor Relations. Please go ahead, Mr. Nelson. DAVID NELSON, HEAD OF GLOBAL IR, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES: Rochelle, thank you very much. Good evening and good morning. I'd like to welcome everyone and thank you for joining us for the TCS earnings call for the second quarter fiscal year 2008. As Rochelle said, I am David Nelson, Head of Investor Relations for TCS. Please note that this call is being webcast through our website at www.tcs.com, and an archive, including transcript, will be available on the site for the duration of the quarter. The financial statements, results presentation and press release are also available on our website. Our leadership team is present on this call to discuss the results. We have with us Mr. Ramadorai, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director. S. RAMADORAI, CEO AND MD, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES: Good evening, good morning, friends. DAVID NELSON: And Mr. Mahalingam, our Chief Financial Officer. S. MAHALINGAM, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, CFO, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES: Good evening, good morning. DAVID NELSON: Mr. Chandrasekaran, our Chief Operating Officer. N. CHANDRASEKARAN, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, COO, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES: Good evening and good morning, everyone. DAVID NELSON: And Mr. Padmanabhan, Head of Global Human Resources. S. PADMANABHAN, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, HEAD OF GLOBAL HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES: Good evening and good morning. DAVID NELSON: And Mr. Phiroz Vandrevala, Head of Global Corporate Affairs. PHIROZ VANDREVALA, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, HEAD OF GLOBAL CORPORATE AFFAIRS, TATA CONSULTANCY SERVICES: Good evening, good morning. DAVID NELSON: Ram and Mahal will begin with a brief

overview of the Company's performance, followed by the Q&A session. As you are aware, TCS does not provide specific revenue and earnings guidance. Furthermore, anything said on this call which reflects our outlook for the future or which can be construed as a forward-looking statement must be viewed in conjunction with the risks that the Company faces. These risks are outlined on the second slide of our results presentation. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Mr. Ramadorai to begin the call. S. RAMADORAI: Thank you, Dave. And friends, as you all know, this quarter has been challenging both from the perspective of currency volatility as well as the subprime issue. I am happy to report that TCS' growth has further accelerated in quarter two. And we have achieved revenues of $2.7b for the first half of this financial year, and for this quarter and ending quarter two, $1.4b or INR5,640 crores. According to the U.S. GAAP, the revenues being at $1.4b, $1.42b to be exact, have risen by 25.83% year on year and 8.4% quarter on quarter. In terms of U.S. GAAP, profits have risen 5.18% quarter on quarter and 25.76% year on year to INR12.469b. So the overall quality of the revenues, contributing to this accelerating growth, is also very good. More importantly, our full services play which we have pioneered has come of age. For the first time in our history, more than 50% of our revenues in this quarter have come from non-ADM services like consulting, infrastructure, BPO and asset leverage solutions. And these are definitely growing at a higher rate than the Company average. We continue to drive our growth through our full services play, aiming at customers in mature markets like North America as well as in the emerging markets. The revenues from the U.S. market have grown in quarter two to 52% of the total revenues. And the early entry which we made into markets like Latin America, APAC and Europe is also beginning to bear fruit. In India we will continue to bid for and win large mission

critical deals. And that's very, very important infinitely with CMC as well. We added 51 clients this quarter and 63%, namely 32 clients, were from non-U.S. geographies, which gives you an indication of the focus we are giving to diversify our revenue base further. The verticals, namely BFSI, telecom and manufacturing, continue to grow higher than the Company average, and transportation is emerging as a big vertical for us. And our accelerated growth has come alongside improved profitability. And how we manage our margins, which will be explained by our CFO, Mahalingam, is due to keeping a strong handle on our costs, which is one of the levers, by executing a competent hedging regime, and increasing the offshore leverage by 190 basis points, and lastly by improving the pricing by about 85 basis points. So, essentially, what this has translated into is an increase in the operating margin -- increase in the operating margin sequentially by 77 basis points, as per the U.S. GAAP. Beyond revenues and profits, TCS continues to set the standard when it comes to managing talent. We were named the best employer in the IT sector for the fourth year in a row. We crossed the 100,000 employee landmark and remain focused on meeting the global career aspirations of our employees. And our attrition rate remained stable at 11.5%, which is the same as quarter one. As an industry pioneer, we will continue to develop new pools of talent. And our first batch of 500 trainees in the science-to-software program, which we have branded as [its name], have successfully completed their training and are being deployed on client projects. We hired a total of 12,523 people this quarter alone and our hiring plans are on track for FY08. And through the compelling projects and assignments which we have, our employees experience certainty in their careers with TCS. Overall, we remain confident of our ability to drive growth in a demand environment for our services, and through services and [accountable] beyond ADM. The value proposition remains strong across markets and industries. Crossing the $2.7b mark in the

first two quarters alone is a great milestone and a benchmark, and we are well positioned to grow on this trajectory. We will continue to watch developments in the context of the subprime issue very closely. But then it is important to note that the financial services business is very diverse, and we will continue to monitor as we go along. So, to recap, our investments in the full services play and early entrance into new markets and geographies, and backed by a global network delivery model, is paying rich dividends, with big deals across geographies and more than 50% of the quarter two growth coming from new services. So we remain confident of our ability to deliver strong growth and we plan on employing additional people this quarter, which Paddy will articulate. But we have made over 22,000 offers across 265 campuses in India, more people to join us next year, namely in the year '08/'09. Thank you so much. S. MAHALINGAM: Thanks, Ram. This is Mahalingam here from -- the Chief Financial Officer. I've -- the market leader, TCS has once again recorded strong and consistent growth during the ending quarter -- September quarter FY2008. This indicates growing acceptance of our resilient and rewarding business model. We mean by this that we continue to diversify the business across geographies, service lines and industries, increasingly improving our positioning with our clients. In U.S. dollar terms, the revenue grew by 11.7% Q1, quarter over quarter, for our international business, 10.8% Q-on-Q in total revenue, and 45.2% year on year in total revenue. It's good to see that our strategy of full services play has matured very well. As Ram said, we now have more than 50% of our revenue coming from new high-growth services. For instance, infrastructure services has grown by 31% Q-on-Q, assurance services at 24%, consulting services at 18%. And similarly, our acquisitions, especially in the area of financial solutions, are bringing in big wins. Of course, many of you have been concerned about the state of the U.S. economy and of the banking and financial services sector,

and Ram has already talked about it. I would like to -- I am pleased to report that both the U.S. market and the BFS sector grew faster than the Company average. However, we'll continue to keep close watch, as Ram said, on the impact of the subprime issue may have on our clients' business. On a rupee basis, revenue grew 8.4% sequentially against the last quarter, 25.8% versus a year ago. Now, let's take a look at the breakdown of our overall revenue growth. Quarter over quarter the growth has been as follows. Volume has grown by 8.19%. Offshore leverage has resulted in 0.99%, which obviously is a dampener from a revenue purpose, but pretty good news from a margin purpose. Pricing has resulted in the revenue going up by 0.85%. In foreign exchange the average rate at which we have converted has resulted in the decline in revenue by 0.51%. And, of course, (inaudible) the hedging profit that we have taken to the revenue, which is at 0.86%. So totally it is 8.4% growth. We will continue to focus on our offshore leverage. This does, however, have a negative impact on our revenue, which has reduced by 99 basis points, as I said, during the quarter. The second key story is our successful and strong financial management that illustrates that TCS can manage in a very volatile environment. Let me now take you through the operating margin, which improved by 77 basis points quarter on quarter. Pricing, productivity and SG&A efficiency resulted in 109 basis points improvement, offshore leverage by 36 basis points improvement. The economic impact of foreign exchange rate changing does have a negative impact of 30 basis points; that is three-zero basis points. Foreign exchange hedging resulted in a positive 79 basis points. And the additional wage costs associated with promotions, as you know, we give increments in the April to June quarter and we promote people in the July to September quarter, and that has resulted in a negative impact of 117; that is one-one-seven basis points. And, therefore, we get an overall positive

margin improvement of 77 basis points. Proactively balancing the foreign exchange is a critical skill, as we have all seen, that is required in volatile times. And I am sure you will agree that we have displayed it. We have adopted a prudent and comprehensive hedging program that works to protect us from foreign currency fluctuations. Since we have hedged on a longer-term basis, this effectively provides us with additional breathing space in an environment of a continuously appreciating rupee. Let me first share here the results of our hedge program for this quarter. Total gains were INR1.027b or 182 basis points. ForEx gains of INR450m or 80 basis points are recorded in the revenue. And the remaining ForEx gains of INR577m or 102 basis points on our hedges are recorded in other income. Therefore, earnings of ForEx gains of 102 basis points that is in other income, operating margin would be 24.8%. In fact, this is what I have been saying in the previous quarter here, during quarter two, that you need to take into account the hedging profit that will get recorded in other income in order to assess the operating margin increase for TCS. And as you can appreciate, 24.85% as the margin in Q2 is essentially targeted as our goal for this year. In addition to this hedging program, we continue a strong focus on cost and pricing management. As a percentage of revenue, combined cost of revenue and SG&A improved by 77 basis points. We remain a strong -- maintain a strong focus on securing pricing commensurate with the value we provide. And of course we'll be covering the detail of pricing during the questions and answers. Finally, I would like to speak with you about our confidence in managing our financial model in an environment of an appreciating rupee and increasing costs. First, we conduct ongoing intensive reviews of our operations and have validated that the current year plan is on track. Second, our hedge accounting, and I am talking about our hedge accounting, in large part ensures that we match hedge gains against

losses of the period, and therefore this evens out the volatility from foreign exchange fluctuations. Third, we keep a close watch on our costs and expenses to continually align expenses and revenue to be in line with the financial model. Given all these and a strong demand environment, I am confident, and I am reiterating it along with Ram, regarding our ongoing financial performance. This is reflected, and I would like to emphasize that, this confidence in our ongoing financial performance is the result of our continued investment in future growth in terms of hiring programs, and Ram has already talked about some figures, infrastructure improvement and our focus on innovation. Thank you. DAVID NELSON: Rochelle, we will now move to questions, please. OPERATOR: All right. We will now begin the question and answer session. (OPERATOR INSTRUCTIONS). The first question comes from the line of Julio Quinteros from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead. JULIO QUINTEROS, ANALYST, GOLDMAN SACHS: Great, thanks. Good evening, guys. I just wanted to check in real quickly on the European operations in particular. It looks like the sequential numbers there might have been moving around a little bit. Can you just walk us through what you are seeing in Europe and what you think the opportunity is here, especially as a potential offset to any U.S. risk as we go forward? S. RAMADORAI: Europe remains a very important market for TCS. We have seen very strong growth in the European market across verticals. We have a good story in terms of financial services, in terms of telecom, in terms of retail, and also utility sectors. We have also won some deals in the transportation sector in the European geography. I would say that the pipeline is strong, and we are pursuing at least six leads for large deals, [considerable] large deals in the European market. So overall I would say that it's a market where we expect to grow strongly. JULIO QUINTEROS: Okay. Great. And then on -- in terms of the longer-term margin drivers, then, at this point when we look forward, can you just

walk us through what you think would be, for the rest of fiscal year 2008, the key margin drivers that we should be focused on here? S. MAHALINGAM: We have already talked about that. We have previously been talking about the pricing, that some of those levers might be there although there are certain conditions now, which we need to be watchful about. We have in this process also shown the onsite to offshore movement of about 1.9%. So that still is a good [one], even in terms of -- in times of appreciating rupee it still makes a lot of sense in terms of moving offshore. The other one is the wage increases are behind us at this time. The only additional wage cost that we are going to get is in terms of new hires and so on. And, therefore, we will have a reduction in that that again will be a margin lever. And the fourth is in -- sometimes we have been working quite a lot in terms of improving the SG&A percentage to reduce from what it is currently. And I believe we will be successful in the coming quarters. JULIO QUINTEROS: Okay. Thank you. S. MAHALINGAM: Productivity is always something that we focus on. We have continuously shown improvements there. JULIO QUINTEROS: Great. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Quinteros. The next question comes from the line of Abi Gami from Banc of America. Please go ahead, sir. ABI GAMI, ANALYST, BANC OF AMERICA: Great, thank you. I'd like to focus on the infrastructure services business. First of all, can you talk about the margins in that business, especially as you've been ramping up a lot of new revenue? If you can also talk a little bit about your onsite/offshore mix within that practice, and is it at an optimized level today or do you feel that there is opportunity to change the mix within that business as well? Thank you. S. RAMADORAI: Thank you, Abi. The infrastructure practice is a very attractive practice, and it's growing significantly. This quarter it is (inaudible) percent

in the infrastructure practice. It is the result of all the large engagements we've signed over the previous quarters; the ramp-ups are happening. At this point, again we are pursuing a number of these. First of all, the outlook on the infrastructure practice from a global point of view is very promising and very good. Coming to the margin, the pricing is very good in the infrastructure practice, number one. Number two is that the area we focus the infrastructure practice is predominantly to [turn] around [most] management of the infrastructure. We don't do a lot of office branches or a lot of [branch infrastructure] work. So given that the offshore ability of the infrastructure services is pretty significant, in some cases we can do 90% plus, that's the target environment in which we should be operating. As you rightly pointed out in your question, definitely we are not at the optimal level because of two reasons. Number one is that we are in the ramp-up mode now at this point in time, so as we are picking up deals we are growing. Second one is that the transitions are happening in many of the deals that we've picked up. So we are not at the optimal level. Definitely there is an opportunity to improve the offshore leverage going forward. ABI GAMI: Okay. Thanks. And as a quick follow up, when you are ramping up a contract in the infrastructure space, are there unusually large amounts of revenue coming in early in the contracts or is it backend weighted or is it -- are the revenues in a contract fairly evenly weighted throughout its life? And also, what is the average life of a contract within that space today? S. RAMADORAI: Okay. There is no unusual seasonality or unusual recognition of trend. Pretty much the contracts are either time and material or fixed rate, which is based on the public condition of that. So there is no upfront licensing fees or anything of the kind which will give a trend and recognize through the [past]. Life of the contracts varies

from three years, five years, that's the kind of duration. ABI GAMI: Thank you very much. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Gami. The next question comes from the line of Mitali Ghosh from DSP Merrill Lynch. Please go ahead. MITALI GHOSH, ANALYST, DSP MERRILL LYNCH: Hi, good evening, and congratulations on a good quarter. Just during the coming quarter, given that it is typically a seasonally weak quarter, could you give us a sense of how we should be thinking about the revenue and margin trend? S. RAMADORAI: No. Mitali, we have been doing reasonably well as far as Q3 is concerned. And the -- it is weak in one sense, in the sense that there are holidays as far as this quarter is concerned, and that is something that we need to keep in mind. We have also been ramping up projects and so on. So to that extent, the volume growth will certainly be there. I am not going to give you any guidance at this moment in time, but certainly we are looking at a difficult quarter. MITALI GHOSH: Should we be looking for margin expansion? S. RAMADORAI: As I said in my opening remarks, the employee costs are behind us -- employee costs are behind us, the expenses connected with recruitment and promotion are behind us. Full text: OPERATOR: Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to the TCS earnings conference call. This is Rochelle, the Chorus Call conference operator. Please note that for the duration of this presentation all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and the conference is being recorded. After the presentation there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions. (Operator Instructions). At this time I would like to turn the conference over to Mr. Kedar Shirali, Director of Investor Relations at TSC. Thank you, and over to you, Mr. Shirali. KEDAR SHIRALI, DIRECTOR, IR, TCS LTD.: Thanks, Rochelle. Good evening, and welcome, everyone. Thank you for joining us today to discuss TCS's financial results for the first quarter of fiscal year 2011 that ended June 30, 2010. This call is being webcast through our website and an archive, including the transcript, will be available on the site for the duration of this quarter. The financial statements, results, presentation and press releases are all available on our website. Our leadership team is here today to discuss, today's -- this quarter's results. We have with us today Mr. N. Chandrasekaran, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director. N. CHANDRASEKARAN, CEO AND MD, TCS LTD: Hello, everyone. KEDAR SHIRALI: Mr. S. Mahalingam, Chief Financial Officer and Executive Director. S. MAHALINGAM, CFO AND EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, TCS LTD: Hello. KEDAR SHIRALI: Mr. Phiroz A. Vandrevala, Head of Global Corporate Affairs and Executive Director. PHIROZ VANDREVALA, HEAD, GLOBAL CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, TCS LTD: Hello, everybody. KEDAR SHIRALI: And Mr. Ajoy Mukherjee, Head of Global Human Resources. AJOY MUKHERJEE, HEAD, GLOBAL HUMAN RESOURCES, TCS LTD: Hi, everyone. KEDAR SHIRALI: As usual, Chandra and Maha will give us a brief overview of the Company's performance and that will be followed by a Q&A session. As you are aware, we do not provide specific revenue or earnings guidance and anything said on this call which reflects our outlook for the future, or which can be construed as a forward-looking statement, must

be reviewed in conjunction with the risks that the Company faces. We have outlined these risks in the second slide of the results presentation emailed to you, and which is also available on our website. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Chandra to begin the proceedings. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Thank you, Kedar. Good morning, good afternoon and good evening, everyone. I'm very pleased to report that we have had a quarter of an all around outperformance. This is a quarter in which we have delivered a volume of over 8%, 8.1%, and a rupee return on revenue of 6.2% and a constant currency revenue of 7.3%. From the historical point of view in absolute numbers, this has been the best quarter since September 2008 and, in terms of constant currency, is the best quarter since September 2007. And this result has come about in a very holistic manner. All our industry segments have done very well. In the past few quarters we saw the BFS segment leading the growth. In this quarter BFS has done extremely well. However, there are other industry segments who have done very well as well, and some who have done better than BFS segment. At least three industry segments have delivered double-digit growth. From a geography point of view the growth has come from all markets. In terms of constant currency, again we have grown all the geographies. US, Canada, Latin America, Europe; both Continental and UK; Middle East, India, Asia Pacific all have delivered growth. However, the growth has been led by both the US and Asia Pacific in this quarter. In terms of the deals that we signed, we've signed 10 large deals and all of the deals are in the non-BFS segment; a couple of deals each from Manufacturing and Hi-Tech industries, and then a deal each in various segments like Retail, Life Sciences & Healthcare, etc. At the beginning of the quarter, very clearly, we knew that there is a significant headwind in terms of margin from the salary increase perspective that only got compounded by the euro

and sterling, causing another headwind. Our teams, both the business teams and the finance teams, have done an incredible job of managing these headwinds and deliver an operating margin of about 27.15%, just 36 basis points below the last quarter -- sequential quarter. In terms of employees, we added a significant number of employees, and considering the demand environment we're going to increase the target from a gross of 30,000 to a gross of 40,000 at this point. As for the BANCS product, it has done extremely well this quarter. Eight of the implementations have gone live and we signed 13 new deals, which are very good. About the deal pipeline, it is very robust, and, again, we have a good number of deals in all markets across industry segments. I would at least specify there are [13] important deals going on, one-third of which are coming out of discretionary spend-critical projects. From the overall environment point of view I'm very well aware, and we, as the management team, are fully cognizant of the macroeconomic conditions, which is very dynamic at this point in time. But our bottom-up data indicates that the momentum is good, the pipeline is good and we are seeing signs of discretionary spending with the type of deals that we are participating in. So there is this disconnect between the macro situation and the bottom-up data. I will just leave it at that. But we remain very positive and we remain closely engaged with our clients, and look forward to good coming months. With those opening remarks I will pass it on to Maha to provide a little more color on the financials, and later on we'll be happy to take any detailed questions. S. MAHALINGAM: Thanks, Chandra. So let me begin by repeating the headline numbers. We posted a revenue of INR82.173b, or 8,217 crores, which is a growth of 6.2% Q-on-Q and 14% year-on-year. In constant currency we grew by 7.3% quarter on quarter. In dollar terms there was a cross-currency impact of 86 basis points negative this quarter, resulting in the reported revenue

of $1.794b; that's a sequential growth of 6.4% and 21.2% on a year-on-year basis. The breakup of quarterly revenue growth on INR terms is, volume growth is plus 8.1%; exchange is negative 1.09%; pricing is negative 0.32%; effort mix, that is shifting from onsite to -- from offshore to onsite, there is a negative 0.48%; total 6.2%. Moving on to costs, if I -- you will -- you might recall from last year's -- last quarter's call that we implemented across-the-board wage increases that went into effect at the start of this financial year. We were able to mitigate the resulting margin impact almost entirely through a combination of three things; better operational leverage through holding many of the non-employee costs at about the same absolute level; this is what I have been saying; the second one is some offshore shift; and the third one is better collections due to which we could reverse some past provisioning for bad debts. That is how we were able to hold the operating margin more or less steady at 27.15% even in a quarter with the severest of margin headwind, suffering only 36 basis points' sequential decline, that too mainly because of currency volatility. The impact of different levers on the operating margin are as follows; currency minus 32 basis points; impact of wage hike minus 215 basis points; offshore shift plus 15 basis points; rate productivity improvement plus 57 basis points; SG&A efficiencies plus 139 basis points. Other income was lower this quarter due to net foreign exchange loss of INR472m, compared to the gains last quarter. Our tax rate also went up this quarter to 19.1%, giving us a net margin of 22.45%. Our DSO for the quarter was 77 days. Cash and liquid funds stood at INR95.2b. In summary, we matched the strong market-leading growth we posted this quarter with an equally strong, robust defense that took a steep wage hike and adverse currency movement in its stride. That speaks of the resilience of our financial model and its ability to deliver in bad times and good. With that, we

can open the lines for questions. KEDAR SHIRALI: Rochelle? OPERATOR: Thank you very much. (Operator Instructions). Our first question is from the line of Balaji Prasad of Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead. BALAJI PRASAD, ANALYST, GOLDMAN SACHS: Thank you. Hi. Good evening, gentlemen. Congratulations on a good set of results. My first question was on your UK growth. This has been quite impressive, at 5.5%, despite the pressure on the pound. Do you see that coming, the negotiation with PADA? And any kind of pullback from BP affecting this? And to what extent could this be affected? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: So as far as the PADA contract is concerned, I think the government is doing the diligence and we are not, at this point in time, aware of any decision where the contract -- any negative decision towards the contract. We are in good discussion with the client and the project is going on as per schedule, and we have a very good contract, but any decision on the PADA contract I don't think will have a negative impact on our performance. BALAJI PRASAD: Okay, that's good to know. Also on BP, have you seen or have you [been seeing] any kind of pullback in projects that you're doing for them that this could reduce in size? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: No. Neither of these relationships are a cause of concern from our point of view but, at any case, at this point in time I don't envisage any negative impact to our performance because of these contracts. BALAJI PRASAD: Okay, that's wonderful. Secondly, can you just give us your collective impressions that you're having when you're discussing pricing with clients globally? Also, what kind -- how receptive have they been to any kind of pricing increase going forward? What are your thoughts on that? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I think we have said repeatedly in the last three, four months that the pricing environment as far as we are concerned is stable and we are looking to maintain the pricing environment in the immediate quarters. And there is definitely a demand pickup, and so

I expect the pricing to go up in the later part of the year. BALAJI PRASAD: Okay, great. Any insight that you can provide on how this has been quite stable at your end while your peers are going through some pricing pressure? We've seen recently one of your peers have warned about a decline in pricing. Any particular insights that you can share with us? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: No, not really. I can only say about us, and I think the pricing environment is stable from our point of view, and we hope to maintain that in the immediate quarters. BALAJI PRASAD: Okay, thank you so much for your time. Good luck for the rest of the year. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Prasad. Our next question is from the line of Edward Caso of Wells Fargo Securities. Please go ahead. EDWARD CASO, ANALYST, WELLS FARGO SECURITIES: Hi, good evening. I was wondering if you could talk a little bit about your Business Process Outsourcing business, particularly now that you've gone a little bit more than a year since the Citi acquisition. And have you been able to leverage that? Any thoughts on current pace of business and so forth? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I think the Business Process Outsourcing business is doing well. In fact, both the prices, the momentum on the BPO have picked up even from the Financial Services clients. We have been able to leverage the Citi deal and we have won more than five clients in the Financial Services segment, where we are continuing to ramp up. And the Citi acquisition per se is ahead of the business plan at this point in time. On the last five quarters' -- last six quarters' performance it is ahead of the business plan. EDWARD CASO: Are you seeing any change in the pace of either interest level or contracts actually being signed? Are your -- is the sales cycle starting to finally shorten a little bit or is this fear of a double-dip recession extending them again? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: See, the sales cycle for BPO is always long and it

will continue to be long. Indeed, it's always a long sales cycle for BPO. I don't want to say long and short. BPO's sales cycle takes a little bit more time than the IT sales cycle in general, and that is the trend we are witnessing. As I said, we are aware of the macro environment and are carefully watching, but we are not seeing any impact of that in our sales cycle or in the delivery cycles or in the ramp-ups. EDWARD CASO: My last question revolves around employee attrition, which clearly has stepped up for TCS in this quarter, as well as for some of your competitors. And we read about significant poaching, as, often, some of the tier two didn't have any bench. We're wondering what steps you're taking to offset that. And has the initial flurry of poaching eased at all, or is the poaching still very high? S. MAHALINGAM: Okay, see, from attrition point of view we have -- it's gone up to about 13.1% at this point in time compared to last quarter, which was at 11.8%, and there are a couple of reasons for that. One is the seasonal part which is -- this is the time some of the people leave for higher studies, so usually, quarter one, the attrition is higher as compared to the remaining quarters in the financial year. The second one is this is the time when we complete our appraisal process and we also announced our increments. So as a result that led to some amount of attrition as a result of that. And the third one, of course, which is industry-growth related and if there is a growth it's bound to reflect on the attrition. But as far as the overall focus is concerned, for us, is on retention, so we are -- we have different schemes, different initiatives to -- for retaining our employees and we have been able to retain our critical talent so, that we have been able to do pretty successfully going. And as far as poaching is concerned, it depends, companies,

for example, we will not go ahead and poach people deliberately from others. It depends on the kind of need that we have and the talent that is available in the market, so it's at that level. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: But, having said that, retention -- employee retention is a key initiative in the Company at this point in time. S. MAHALINGAM: Yes. EDWARD CASO: Great, thank you very much. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Caso. Ladies and gentlemen, before we take the next question we'd like to request participants to limit their questions to one during the initial round of questions and answers; there are several participants waiting for their turn. Our next question is from the line of Joseph Foresi of Janney Montgomery Scott. Please go ahead. JEFF ROSSETTI, ANALYST, JANNEY MONTGOMERY SCOTT: Hello, this is Jeff Rossetti calling on behalf of Joseph Foresi. I just wanted to follow up on the question regarding attrition. Could you -- you mentioned that the gross hiring guidance was increased to 40,000 from 30,000. Is there a certain amount attributed to increased attrition and a certain amount attributed to expected growth? UNIDENTIFIED COMPANY REPRESENTATIVE: I think the gross hiring increase that we have done it is primarily being driven by the demand growth that we see. JEFF ROSSETTI: Okay, so not too much related to the -- on the attrition side? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: No. JEFF ROSSETTI: And on Continental Europe I know you mentioned that there was a constant currency growth for all geographies, but could you maybe discuss what kind of demand you're seeing within Continental Europe and how that has changed in the last month or two? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Of all markets the Continental Europe market has had the slowest growth in this quarter. The demand environment in Continental Europe is good, but the sales cycle in Continental Europe also tends to be a little longer. We expect that it'll get better from here. For example, in this quarter we have had a constant currency growth of about 1.2% in Continental growth and we expect things to get better from here.

JEFF ROSSETTI: Okay. Thank you very much, and congratulations on the quarter. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Foresi. Our next question is from the line of Anthony Miller of TechMarketView. Please go ahead. ANTHONY MILLER, ANALYST, TECHMARKETVIEW: Yes, I'd like to just clarify a bit more about the European scene. You just said that the constant currency growth in Continental Europe was 1.2%. Can you just give what the UK constant currency growth was in comparison, please? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: 5.1%. ANTHONY MILLER: That was, sorry, 5.1%? Okay. Because you -- sorry, yes. So you said that even though Continental Europe was 1.2% you felt confident that things will get better from here. What is it that gives you that confidence? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Just based on the conversations we have with clients and the engagements we are pursuing. ANTHONY MILLER: Okay. And, just finally, you also mentioned that you had a number of BANCS deals; you signed 13 new BANCS deals in the quarter. Can you say which geographies those were in and what the sort of specific applications they were? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: They are well distributed across the globe. And there are four or five core banking deals, there are deals in the insurance sector, there are deals in the market infrastructure and custody area. ANTHONY MILLER: Okay, thanks very much indeed. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Miller. Our next question is from the line of Mitali Ghosh of Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Please go ahead. MITALI GHOSH, ANALYST, BANK OF AMERICA MERRILL LYNCH: Yes, hi. Good evening and congratulations on a great quarter. Chandra, if you could just give us some color on the trends in the Banking vertical, because last few quarters we've seen strong growth led by more general integrations-related work. I just wanted to understand is that leveling off. Also, I thought you mentioned that there were no new BFS deals in the large deals that you signed this quarter so, again, just trying to understand what sort of demand you're seeing there. And, finally, if you could share what the constant currency growth was for the

Banking vertical this quarter. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: The constant growth rate for banking vertical is 6.5% this quarter and, Banking vertical, the demand environment continues to be good. And it is not that we are not signing the banking deals. There were a number of deals we have signed in the banks' product-related deals. In terms of pure IT services we are pursuing a good number of deals in the Banking and Financial Services vertical. In fact, of all the deals that we are pursuing I would say that Banking and Financial Services has more number of deals than other sectors. So I would say that the outlook for Banking and Financial Service and Insurance sector looks good. MITALI GHOSH: Just as a follow up to that, if you could give us some color in terms of what is the kind of demand you're seeing from the banks, in terms of nature of projects, now that probably integration work is more or less getting completed. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: We are seeing some transformation deals; deals in the area of compliance, deals in the area of re-platforming. When I say re-platforming, changing from legacy to (inaudible) application that is interest in terms of analytics. And there are also deals coming in within [more] infrastructure management space so -- and then there are deals in the BPO space from the Financial Services sector so I think the type of deals very (inaudible). MITALI GHOSH: Okay, thanks, that's very helpful. And overall on the pipeline you mentioned that the specialty products is a large chunk. How has that changed over the last three months? Has the proportion in the pipeline actually moved up? Also, if you could comment on what is the mix in the pipeline from new customers, maybe perhaps first-time offshorers, and from existing outsourcing deals coming up for re-bid. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Okay. In terms of the pipeline, definitely the deals from discretionary spend proportion of that in the pipeline has gone up. In fact, three quarters -- last three quarters until the previous quarter we have said that the most of the

deals are non-discretionary point of nature, efficiency-related in nature, but we are seeing deals coming out of the discretionary spend in the pipeline. Clearly, that is a positive that I'm happy to report this quarter. Then, from the point of view of the existing versus new clients, I think it's a good healthy mix. Most of the deals that I am talking about are either new clients or clients where we have a smaller percent and we are having an opportunity to increase our percent but -- although there are also deals with the existing customers that we are pursuing. I don't know whether I answered your question or did you have anything else. MITALI GHOSH: Yes, just on -- is there a large chunk coming from existing deals where you're perhaps gaining share from incumbents? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Whenever there is a deal that is in the area of efficiency or taking cost out there will always be incumbents, okay, so those type of deals always face incumbents plus new providers. But the discretionary spend deals are probably -- are all new projects where we are competing. MITALI GHOSH: Thanks. Just one last question on pricing. I heard your comments earlier. I just wanted to understand what is the risk of volume discount perhaps kicking in as some of the older renegotiations -- as a result of some of the older renegotiations in the past few quarters. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Mitali, I think all I would say is that we believe we can maintain the pricing at the current levels. MITALI GHOSH: Okay, that's very helpful. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, Miss. Ghosh. Our next question is from the line of Sandeep Shah of ICICI Securities. Please go ahead. SANDEEP SHAH, ANALYST, ICICI SECURITIES: Yes, just on the attrition, if we look at this quarter the percentage of three-year -- more than three year of experience has moved up by almost 300 basis points. Is it fair to say that we are realizing attrition more towards less than three years' experience, fact? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I think the way to look at

that is also there has been significant lateral adds this quarter. And our HR team has done a stupendous job of meeting the volume growth demand by ensuring that we've hired a large number of people and provide the right mix to the engagements so that, to some extent, will have a distraction. And also in this quarter, traditionally -- though I don't have the exact number to give you on the call, traditionally in the first quarter we have people who have been -- who have joined for one or two years quitting for higher studies, and that adds to the attrition. So a portion of that that you see is due to that. So these are the two explanations I can give you. And obviously if you want more data you can contact Ajoy later on and he will happily share. SANDEEP SHAH: No, this is helpful. Second, in terms of the new deals which are coming, are they coming at a higher than the Company average billing rate? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Why don't you -- why don't we just leave it at the fact that the pricing is going to be maintained and we are looking at an upward bias at the end of the quarter. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay, okay. And just, Maha -- N. CHANDRASEKARAN: At the end of the year. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay. And, Maha, just on the hedging, can you give us a color in terms of the outstanding old covers and any new covers taken for the coming quarter or for the quarter beyond Q2 FY '11? S. MAHALINGAM: They are well written about, standing of the old covers. This quarter we will have something like $75m of old cover which was taken at, I think, INR42.13; that'll come back. And then the balance remaining is something like $30m over a period of time. So then it'll all be over. And as far as the current hedges are concerned, we took some hedges for Q2 and something more a little later, but they're all reasonably small. We have outstanding hedge of about $455m. SANDEEP

SHAH: Okay, okay. And any color in terms of the average strike rate for these --? S. MAHALINGAM: For those ones they are combination of dollar and euro and so on. As far as the dollar is concerned, the best strike is about INR46.33. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay, okay. And just, Maha, in terms of the margin, in the coming quarter we may have a headwind to promotion, as well as there could be a normalization of the provision for doubtful debt. So I'm not asking for a guidance but just in terms of a direction of the margin. Do you believe it's sustainable in the coming quarter? S. MAHALINGAM: As I have said, our intent -- we've always said we don't give guidance. But our intent is that it should be around the 27% mark. You have correctly put it, the wage increase comes in two places for us, April to June, we have got the increments, and July to September, we have got the promotions, and therefore it will kick in. So that is a headwind that we have. We are also in a growth phase in data, etc. and Ajoy has said, there is a big recruitment program that is going on. And therefore, there are going to be additional employee costs that are coming in. And as you may have noticed, and so on, we have also not cut down on some of the sales related costs, and so on. Some of the costs have gone up. Quite a lot of the costs we have controlled. So these are there. But in a growth environment, we believe with the liquid cost control measures and the productivity improvements and so on, we will be able to take on these headwinds. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay. So we still maintain the internal target of 27% EBIT margin for the full year. S. MAHALINGAM: Oh no. No guidance. No guidance at all. These are all aspirational statements. And I just want to also add that when I said, we will be able to take on -- I'm not saying that we will

be able to take on. So we will -- you know the direction of the (inaudible). The typical quarter, where we have had a 215 basis point issue with this wage hike, we have still managed to restrict the decline to 36 basis points. SANDEEP SHAH: Okay. Thanks, and congrats once again on a good set of results. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Shah. Our next question is from the line of Nitin Padmanabhan of Indiabulls Securities. Please go ahead. NITIN PADMANABHAN, ANALYST, INDIABULLS SECURITIES: Yes, hi. Thanks for taking my question. The telco vertical seems to have grown pretty well this quarter. What are the trends there and how do you see that, going forward? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: The telco vertical has done well. But you should also note that the telco vertical had the biggest fall over the last few quarters. So it's coming off that and it has shown good growth. And I think my plan is good. Our ramp-ups are good, so positive good growth. But I'm not going to give you a number. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Sure. And with reference to constant currency for manufacturing, how did it look? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Manufacturing on a constant currency basis delivered close to 4%, 390 basis points. NITIN PADMANABHAN: Sure. Perfect, thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you, Mr. Padmanabhan. Our next question is from the line of Diviya Nagarajan of UBS. Please go ahead. DIVIYA NAGARAJAN, ANALYST, UBS: Hi. Congrats on a good set of numbers. Just a couple of questions. I think we've seen -- we seem to have seen a good revival in some of your troubled sectors, notably manufacturing and telecom. What do you think has driven this revival? And how sustainable do you think this will be, going forward? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: I think, as I have said, we are happy that these verticals have come back. But you know the macro situation can [hurt] these verticals. That's only a macroeconomic effect. But as we see today, the data points we have, we are positive of growth in these verticals. The pipeline is good. And we are having good

conversations with clients. But these are verticals which are susceptible to the macroeconomic situations. We just need to watch that. But it looks good at this point. DIVIYA NAGARAJAN: My second question relates to the strength of this overall recovery. We seem to have been surprised, quarter after quarter, by the kind of volume growth of the large [caps] such as you also have reported. My question is, is this -- should we view this as the beginning of another wave of offshoring where you will continue to gain market share at a much faster pace than expected. And if that's happening, where do you think that the new pockets of penetration are opening up for you? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: We're going to wait for one more quarter at least before commenting on this. DIVIYA NAGARAJAN: Sure, thanks. And Mahal, a bookkeeping question. Could you split your other income into ForEx and the others, please. S. MAHALINGAM: Other income, it's about INR47 crores in terms of the losses. And the balance is really the treasury income. DIVIYA NAGARAJAN: Thanks. And once again, a great quarter and all the best. the Company faces. We have outlined these risks on the second slide of the results presentation, which is available on our website. If you take the geography perspective, we have grown in all the markets in which we operate. Our emerging markets, Middle East, Africa, and India and Asia Pacific have delivered a double-digit dollar growth. And our major markets, namely US, UK and Continental Europe have delivered high single-digit growth rate. And we have had very good growth coming from BFSI and manufacturing industries as well. And in all the other sectors also, we were pretty happy with the performance. expanded the revenue band, the number of customers in the revenue bands of $10m, $20m, $15m and $100m handsomely, in each and every band. Then if you look at the deal closures, it has been pretty good. We at least signed 10 key deals, large deals this quarter. And they have been pretty broad based. And if you look at the deal pipeline, the pipeline is very good, robust at this point in time. And if you take the top 15 deals that we are chasing, it's again well distributed across US, UK, Europe and the emerging markets and similarly in terms of the industries in which we operate. The utilization has been pretty good and excluding trainees we have maintained it at about 83.4% -- 83.2% as we had said in the last earnings call. If you look at the overall environment going forward, I would like to make the following observations. The first is that the global environment is uncertain and it will continue to be so for time to come, primarily because things are different in different markets. There are markets in which unemployment is the issue. There are markets that you have inflation problems, markets in which there is civil unrest. And there are markets in which there are natural calamities, so all kinds of things are going on. how we partner with clients as a firm today is very different from what we used to do a few years ago. And this varies according to industry. If you look at another industry, it is supply chain. So the transformation agenda is our ability to partner with customers in solving a high-level business problem and capturing the downstream revenue. It requires skills in enterprise solutions. It requires consulting skills, domain skills, architecture skills and execution skills. And we are able to bring all of that to bear in both capturing the demand, as well as executing the demand. In dollar terms, our revenue of $2.412b is a quarter-on-quarter growth of 7.4% and year-on-year growth of 34.4%. Constant currency revenue was $2.383b, a growth of 6.2% quarter on quarter. The breakup of our quarterly revenue growth in Indian rupee terms is as follows. Volume growth was plus 7.45%. Exchange is plus 10 basis points. Realization is minus [50] basis points. Effort mix is minus 75 basis points. And it comes to 6.3%. Moving on to margin, you might recall that in April we had given a 12% to 14% wage hike in India and varying amounts in other countries. As expected, we felt an immediate impact on the first quarter of operating margin. Despite higher utilization and operational leverage from top-line growth, this

quarter's EBIT margin declined 2.1%, as we have reported, sequentially to 26.2%. I want to just make one observation here. We have moved from US GAAP to IFRS. And therefore, at the time of drawing last year's -- last quarter's IFRS accounts, the margin had improved slightly, to a one-time adjustment of 28.3%. But that benefit we don't have in this quarter. I'm just emphasizing to say that because we had a difference of 23 basis points between the two, the real margin drop has been 1.9%. But I will let that remain as -- The impact of different levers on the operating margin is as follows. Currency is minus 9 basis points. Impact of wage hikes is 251 basis points. Offshore shift is plus 7 basis points. Rate productivity improvement is plus 115 basis points. SG&A efficiencies, the first component is provisioning for bad debt. That is minus 15 basis points. Others, minus 61 basis points. And therefore, we come up with a difference of minus 214 basis points. On net income, our other income was higher this quarter from foreign exchange gains of INR797m, compared to the last quarter. As expected, our tax rate went up following the expiry of software technology past scheme benefits or what we refer to as (inaudible). And the tax rate now is 22.7%, giving us a net margin of 22%. Lastly, our DSO for the quarter was 83 days. Cash and liquid funds stood at INR105.2b. In conclusion, we have made a very good start in the opening moments of this current inning to use a cricket term. The growth momentum continues and our execution engine is humming along nicely, well-placed [advantage that demand] very well. In fact there are a few deals during the last three or four months that we had to not participate, and kind of de-qualify it from our pipeline, primarily because the deal structures were different and there are others who want to do those deals. So, I can only tell you that we try and keep the business model simple. PANKAJ KAPOOR: Okay, great. Thank you and all the best. OPERATOR: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Ashwin Mehta from Nomura. Please go ahead. ASHWIN MEHTA, ANALYST, NOMURA: Hi, congratulations on a good set of numbers. I had a question, typically Q2 has a higher proportion of freshers but given that you added less than 2% headcount in this

quarter and are running at 83% utilization, do you see either of the possibilities utilizations temporarily being higher than your guided range or more up front lateral hiring in Q2 for the [ramps] that you see? AJOY MUKHERJEE: See 2Q I said we would be doing between 17 to 20 so that is the gross addition that we will have. At the moment given the kind of demand that we have I think we do have sufficient -- the manpower that we need in order to fulfill that demand including the hiring that we will do in 2Q. ASHWIN MEHTA: Okay, but in terms of pattern 2Q will just still be skewed significantly towards freshers? AJOY MUKHERJEE: In terms of pattern yes it will be skewed towards the fresher's. It will be somewhere around 50/50 kind of a split. ASHWIN MEHTA: Okay. AJOY MUKHERJEE: Okay. ASHWIN MEHTA: Thanks a lot. OPERATOR: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Sanil Daptardar from Sentinel Investments. Please go ahead. SANIL DAPTARDAR, ANALYST, SENTINEL INVESTMENTS: Thanks. Just wondering about how do you plan to use your cash? Your cash balance continues to build up on your books. Could you just give a color on that? KEDAR SHIRALI: How do I want to -- how do we want to use the cash? I think that -- N. CHANDRASEKARAN: There are two things one is that currently we are intending to make our investments. And from acquisition point of view we will keep looking. So if there is a right effect we will look at acquisitions, acquisition is definitely something that we keep looking. And whenever we find the right asset we will need the cash. SANIL DAPTARDAR: Any plans to increase the dividends or stock buyback or any other -- other than those acquisitions any other use for the cash? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Our dividends are one of the benchmarks in the industry, we currently pay very handsome dividends and whenever we feel that there is excess cash and we don't need it then we give special dividend, like we did last year.

So, that's our policy. UNIDENTIFIED COMPANY REPRESENTATIVE: At the moment, nothing is being [devised]. SANIL DAPTARDAR: Okay, on the volume growth that you talked about, 7.4% I guess, just could you give us a little color on what was the sectoral breakdown. What sectors contributed the most to the volume growth and how do you see going forward, when you're talking about healthy pipelines between different sectors. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Still retail, hi-tech contributed significantly to the volume growth. As for less, telecom and BFSI and manufacturing. SANIL DAPTARDAR: And when you look at the pipeline, where are you seeing the most healthy pipeline? What sectors are you seeing the pipeline? N. CHANDRASEKARAN: It's pretty distributed. If I take the top 15 deals, five of them in BFSI, telecom, manufacturing, utilities and travel two each, then we have a couple of deals in media and hi-tech. SANIL DAPTARDAR: Okay. Just a last question on the pricing, up till this quarter you had a 50 bps decline in pricing. You talked about you are getting price increases but that may take some time to materialize. Can it be inferred that you might be bidding for some low value work or that is not the case? S. MAHALINGAM: I think I have given enough data points for you to believe that we are doing a very high quality business. You know 50 basis points is neither here nor there, you know that's right even in the previous quarter when we had a 1% increase that was of -- we didn't make much of it. So these are all minor (multiple speakers). N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Yes. I just want you to notice that today we have a margin of 26.2% which is pretty good margin. And we have been very careful in choosing the deals that we want to do. And we continue to make investments and opening new markets. And as I said our transformation engagement pipeline is going up. So there are enough data points I've given you on how we are shaping our business. SANIL DAPTARDAR: Good. Thanks a lot. OPERATOR: Thank

you. The next question is from the line of [Pritesh Hora] from [Equinox]. Please go ahead. PRITESH HORA, ANALYST, EQUINOX: My question has been answered. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Sandip Agarwal from Antique Stock Broking. Please go ahead. SANDIP AGARWAL, ANALYST, ANTIQUE STOCK BROKING: Yes, hi Chandra and Maha and your team. Congratulations for a very good quarter. Just one question, you have said that you'll be adding more number of freshers probably in the second quarter. So, just wanted to have some light on the utilization part, what I believe is that in second quarter you will have 400 basis point kind of utilization decline if you take into account these trainees. Is this correct? Is my assumption correct? AJOY MUKHERJEE: See, we in general want to operate 82% to 84% excluding trainees. Including trainees, if the trainee influx will increase definitely you will see a decline in the utilization including trainees. SANDIP AGARWAL: Yes, correct. So, what I am -- I am -- I believe is that next quarter probably there will be some decline from the current level, so that's what I believe. So is my assumption correct that's what I am asking here? AJOY MUKHERJEE: Your assumption is right for including trainees but not for excluding trainees. SANDIP AGARWAL: Okay, thanks, thanks. Thanks a lot. OPERATOR: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, due to time constraints that was the last question. I would now like to hand the floor back to Mr. Shirali for closing comments. Please go ahead, sir. KEDAR SHIRALI: Chandra. N. CHANDRASEKARAN: Thank you. Thank you all for joining this call. And in summary I would like to say that we have started the year quite well with an exceptional quarter. We are happy with both financial numbers and more importantly the operating numbers. We are seeing a very broad based growth. It has come across markets and across industries. And we are seeing the kicking in of the discretionary spend from the deal closers. And we are seeing the demand environment continue to hold.

And we are happy with the way our business has increased with all our existing customers who added more than -- more customers in the $20m band, $50m band and $100m band, across all the bands, which is very satisfying. And we already talked about utilization which we'll keep at 80% to 84%. And overall I think we are off to a good start and we're happy with where we are. Thank you very much. And thank you for your support. OPERATOR: Thank you, gentlemen of the management. Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of TCS that concludes this conference call.
