And with that I will turn the call over to Don Fowler. DON FOWLER, CEO, SUMTOTAL SYSTEMS INC.: Thank you Neil. We're pleased to highlight another quarter of strong performance. This mirrors in many ways what you've seen over recent quarters. In fact our Q2 performance extends our streak to four consecutive quarters of double-digit, year-over-year revenue growth and solid profitability. Similarly it is our third consecutive quarter with growth in deferred revenue. Our Q2 performance is a direct result of sticking to the strategy that we have discussed in recent quarters. To recap the three main components of that strategy are, first, building our core business at a rate equal to or higher than the industry's growth rate. Second, developing our OEM business as an incremental growth opportunity for SumTotal. And third, expanding our application reach to include more of the talent management market through partnerships, internal start-ups and strategic M&A work. With regard to the first strategic component we are pleased with the amount of business we are seeing from across a number of vertical industries such as financial services, manufacturing and retail. The latest release of our enterprise platform SumTotal 7.2 includes a number of features that helps customers in these and other vertical industries meet their training challenges that are tied to compliance, readiness, managing employee performance and aligning an individual's goals with a company's overall business objectives. We continue to grow our base business through initiatives aimed at selling into our large installed base. Q2 saw about 60% of our revenue come from this area. Our customer base presents opportunities for us to take learning management systems that are being used on a divisional level for a few thousand employees and expand those to enterprise-level platforms serving tens of thousands of workers. a large brokerage firm and a top-five US bank. The bank had our solution in place for 10,000 users and a competitor's product across other divisions. We were able to leverage our departmental solution, beat out the competitors offering and win the enterprise wide business with SumTotal 7.2 for a rollout to 155,000 users. New customers continue to contribute to our results as well. For instance in Q2 we had 20 new enterprise deals at an average selling price of $530,000. Our international business comprised 15% of our overall business for the quarter. This is consistent with what we've seen over the past two quarters. As part of our strategy we have told you that we are making investments in sales and marketing programs in India and China. Sometime after the first of the year you should see our international investments start to pay off with a higher percentage of business from international. We see this as a terrific growth opportunity for us to leverage our expertise and brand, around the world. By developing programs tailored to upgrading our installed base, selling enterprise deals, new enterprise deals and developing international markets we feel our core business will grow at a rate equal to or greater than the industry averages. This emphasis is also having a positive effect on our recurring revenue which represented 475% of total revenue in Q2. As for the second component of our strategy, the OEM initiative. We announced a contract at the beginning of the quarter with Accelerate HRO for $13.3 million over a period of eight years to provide our learning and performance management platform to a leading provider of product services and technologies, supporting the health care industry. In addition to this deal we also won a contract through our partnership with Hewitt to provide our solution to a regional power company. The third component of our growth strategy involves building the business by expanding into other sectors of talent management. I along with senior members of our executive team have spent, and will continue to spend time exploring partnerships, internal start-ups and M&A

activities. As you know, on June 1st we filed a Shelf Registration Statement with the Securities & Exchange Commission for a maximum aggregate of $75 million. Over the past four quarters I believe we've delivered the kind of predictable results that should increase shareholder value as we continue to grow our revenues and profits. The three components of our strategy are designed to allow us to grow our current business and expand into more sectors of talent management with excellent growth rate over time. Industry analysts have projected high growth rates for the overall talent management sector and we plan to take advantage of this opportunity. Neil will now cover the financials for the second quarter and guidance for the third quarter. NEIL LAIRD: Thank you Don. During the second quarter we saw continued strength in the markets we serve. Towers [Perry], Alticore the parent of Amway and Ericsson AV, demonstrate our success in winning large enterprise deals. The following analysis includes non-GAAP numbers first and then GAAP numbers. So, on a non-GAAP basis our revenue was $26.5 million which was 66% higher than the $16 million we reported in the second quarter of 2005. I get many questions about our organic growth rate because clearly the acquisition of Pathlore contributes greatly to this increase. Coming up with an organic growth rate is not as simple as it sounds as we have converted some Pathlore prospects and customers to SumTotal. However our best estimate is that approximately $6 million of revenue in the second quarter of 2006 and also in the first quarter of 2006 came from the Pathlore installed base. If you exclude this $6 million from our revenue of $26.5 million the resulting number of $20.5 million represents an organic increase of 28% compared to last year. I want to remind everyone that last year's second quarter results were disappointing and this type of organic growth is not forecasted on an ongoing basis. The first quarter growth rate using the same approach was 19% and our guidance, that I'll discuss later for the third quarter, implies an organic growth rate of somewhere between 10% and 20%. I think that this range is more reflective of a realistic go forward target. Again, this range is consistent with industry analyst's estimates for the broad market and its size that we have met and will continue to meet our goal of growing at better than industry rates. License revenue in the third quarter, also on a non-GAAP basis was $8.3 million which was 60% higher than last year's second quarter revenue of $5.2 million. Approximately $1.5 million of this came from the Pathlore base so the estimated organic growth rate on licenses was around 30%. The growth in service revenue compared to last year was a little lower than license growth. Given the number of large deals we booked in the second quarter I expect strong service revenue growth in the

next two quarters as we complete these implementations. In the short-term I expect that service revenue will grow faster than license revenue. One aspect of our revenue picture that is also worth pointing out is the strength of our recurring revenue. We continue to sell a mix of perpetual and subscription licenses. And have also had good success in selling hosting subscriptions. In total our recurring revenue which includes ASP and maintenance as well as subscriptions for licenses and hosting, has increased from 37% of revenue in 2004 to 42% in 2005 and 47% in the first half of 2006. Our gross margin on an non-GAAP basis increased from $10.5 million in 2005 second quarter to $17.9 million this year. This is a 70% increase on a 66% revenue increase. So we continue to achieve economies of scale and improve the percentage gross margin from 66% to 68%. We made progress in our service margins during the quarter improving to a 54% gross margin compared to 53% in the first quarter. However this is still lower than the 55% level we achieved in the second quarter of last year. As discussed last quarter we've invested in building our service infrastructure and this caused a temporary dip in service margins. We started to see improvement in the second quarter and I expect this upward trend to continue in the coming quarters. Operating expenses for the quarter were $15.6 million compared to $12.7 million a year ago. This increase was only 23% compared to the 66% revenue increase and reflects the full realization of the synergies from the Pathlore acquisition. Our first quarter expenses were $16.4 million and this sequential decline was primarily in G&A as we have completed the additional expenses associated with SOX 404 compliance, changing our auditors and the legal expenses relating to patent litigation. In our Non-Operating Income and Expense line we reported foreign exchange gains of approximately $200,000 which offset the losses that we had recorded in previous quarters. We have now implemented a hedging program that should reduce fluctuations caused by exchange rate movements in future

quarters. Our non-GAAP net income was $2.3 million or $0.09 per share compared to a net income of $900,000 or $0.04 per share in the first quarter and a loss of $2.4 million or $0.11 per share in last year's second quarter. Moving on to our GAAP Income Statements, we recorded a $1 million stock based compensation charge. A $2.2 million charge for the amortization of intangibles and we reduced revenue by $1.4 million as a result of the deferred revenue write down on the Pathlore acquisition. The GAAP Statement of Operations shows a 58% year-on-year revenue growth and a net loss that improved from $3.4 million in last year's second quarter or $0.16 per share to a loss of $2.3 million or $0.09 in the current quarter, most recent quarter. The balance sheet and cash flow also showed good improvements in the quarter. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments increased by $1.7 million during the quarter. Cash flow from operations in the quarter was approximately $4.5 million. And we used $2 million of that for capital expenditures primarily for our new facility in India and a further $1.1 million for the quarterly payment under our term loan. Receivables increased by $700,000 last quarter but we are still well down on the year end level and these are well under control. DSO based on the non-GAAP revenue was 71 days, unchanged from the first quarter, and down from 84 days at year end. Deferred revenue also increased to a record $28.1 million. This is higher than the end of the first quarter by $1.7 million and up from year end by $1.4 million. It's also 43% higher than the year ago. I will digress briefly to discuss stock options. The topic that has been on many people's minds over the past few weeks and months. The company decided, in the light of issues that other company's have reported, to carry out a review of past practices of SumTotal. Our review looked at the processes that have been followed since the company's IPO of Asymetrix in June of 1998. I am

pleased to report that we have found no material problems that would require us to restate our previously reported results. Looking forward our guidance for the third quarter is for revenue of between $26 and $28 million on a non-GAAP basis. Net income is forecast for between $2 million or $0.08 per share and $3 million or $0.12 per share. This success comes from our ability to execute to the plan which Don mentioned earlier. To elaborate on some of the steps that we've taken, we've created marketing programs and initiatives that show how our SumTotal 7 platform can help our customers meet their compliance, readiness and performance management needs. These are some of the key drivers for the purchase of talent management systems. According to IDC SumTotal's talent management solution gives HR executives an integrated approach to overcoming these challenges. The market programs and product features we have designed for these areas are paying off. We are building more pipeline and winning more deals. More than 200 customers have purchased SumTotal 7 since its release in December of 2004. As a side note, two of these customers have been running on the Pathlore platform and more than 20 Pathlore customers are currently in our pipeline for an upgrade to SumTotal 7. These customers and others among our installed base have chosen to upgrade to SumTotal 7 because

they are looking for a broad set of solutions to tackle these key business problems. We continue to see the retail sector adopt SumTotal 7. The acute need in retail is employee on boarding, the ability to hire employees quickly and make them productive. Typically our solution helps to compress the time it takes to train workers to do their jobs once they're hired. To cut the time customers spend at the point of sale and to boost the accuracy with which employees take customer's orders. We now have more than 15 customers who have deployed the SumTotal learning and performance management solutions. contribution to revenue for the sixth consecutive quarter. Satyam's ability to architect innovative and extensible solution frameworks in this area has led to higher growth, enhanced customer intimacy and strong brand equity. It is also a reflection of our increased involvement in partnering with customers to deal with transformational issues effectively. the demand in marketplace, which we believe is fuelled by increasing budgets for IT spend and driving a number of global outsourcing deals. The corresponding EPS growth for fiscal 2007 is revised upwards to 37.0%. My question has been answered. Thank you. OPERATOR: Thank you very much sir. Next question comes from the line of Mr. Harmendra Gandhi with BRICS Securities. HARMENDRA GANDHI, ANALYST, BRICS SECURITIES: Hi, good evening. When do we see steady ramp up in Nipuna? One quarter we see good growth and things, another quarter where we see slowing down of growth on a quarter-to-quarter basis. Do you think sometime, by what time in future we may see that kind of growth where we have a steady quarter-to-quarter growth in Nipuna? VENKATESH RODDAM: This is Venkatesh here. I think the reason why you see the ups and downs of that is on account of the ramp up that we are currently undergoing on a quarter-to-quarter basis. For example, if you look at the growth in Q3 versus Q2, that's purely on account of our [600 fee] engagement that we are ramping up to, during the course of Q3. So that is the reason exactly why you are

seeing an up and down in the ramp up. However, when you look at the revenue forecast and the EBITDA forecast for the year, the trend is extremely positive. And I think from Q1 of next year onwards you will see a steady growth rate on a quarter-on-quarter basis. HARMENDRA GANDHI: Okay. And same for the losses actually, net profit on net losses, they are fluctuating so much from quarter-to-quarter. VENKATESH RODDAM: This is primarily driven by investments made during the course of the year to support the revenue that has come in. Most [inaudible] business that has been booked in the course of Q2, Q3 and Q4 of this year that is in the pipeline will yield results during the course of Q1 onwards for next year. So in that context these are investments leading to revenues and profits moving forward. So it is a conscious decision that we have taken in terms of what needs to get invested for future growth. HARMENDRA GANDHI: Okay. So from Q1 next year you will see steady growth and steady margins also. VENKATESH RODDAM: I would anticipate so. HARMENDRA GANDHI: Thanks a lot. OPERATOR: Thank you very much sir. At this moment I would like to hand over the floor to Christy to conduct the Q&A session for participants at WebEx International Center. Thank you and over to Christy. OPERATOR: Thank you moderator. We will now begin the Q&A session for participants connected to the WebEx International Bridge. [OPERATOR INSTRUCTIONS]. Your first question is from Trip Chowdhry with Global Equities. TRIP CHOWDHRY, ANALYST, GLOBAL EQUITIES: Thank you. And, again, a good execution in a difficult exchange market. Two quick questions, first, regarding the Infrastructure business. I was wondering can you give a split between two processes. One is usually build and maintain, other is usually build and transfer. And since there is a drop, I believe that most of your implementation may be build and transfer it back to the client rather than build and maintain it yourself. Any thoughts on that? RAM MYNAMPATI: This is Ram Mynampati here. You know, it

goes back to the discussion related to whether a solution is annuity type or whether it has got a finite period within which the service becomes valid. If we take over the maintenance of a specific service, not necessarily the Infrastructure, but services closer to Infrastructure, that has to be longer term in nature, and that is what you are referring to as building and operating if you will. But if there is an engagement that calls for a software rollout, or a migration of some kind across the enterprise that is going to be an instance where we are taking responsibility for a specific task. And we will turn over the responsibility for execution and operation if you will of that back to the organization, because our job ends with bringing the Infrastructure up to a certain level where we have been contracted to do so. I am not so sure whether there are going to be instances where we are building an infrastructure and turning all the infrastructure, because that's not what we refer to in Infrastructure Management Services. I think it's more in the way the services are defined and understood. TRIP CHOWDHRY: That's fine. Second is regarding the banking and financial sector. It does seem like the competition may have got heated up in that space because of Oracle's acquisition of i-flex. Then Infosys having its own [cynical] product line and TCS having its own banks offering, which is more asset leverage kind of a solution. I was wondering does Satyam have any initiatives in that space where they have already pre-packaged solutions that they can deliver and probably be a little bit more competitive? And thanks again and congratulations on good execution in a difficult exchange environment. B. RAMALINGA RAJU: Thank you. The answer to that is we don't have any current plans of bringing out a solution of our own to banking and financial services space. We -- while that is a stated strategy for some organizations, our strategy is to remain product agnostic and find the right alliances with the right product vendors

that ultimately enables us to deliver the best solutions to our customers in a [competitive] way. So we have not invested in building a solution of our own. We would like to remain product agnostic and provide those services are that are best of the breed in the market. Can we move on to the next question please? OPERATOR: The next question is from Julio Quinteros with Goldman Sachs. JULIO QUINTEROS, ANALYST, GOLDMAN SACHS: Hey guys. My question is actually related to pricing. Can you talk about what the environment is like for you guys in pricing? What are you seeing on new clients? I haven't heard you guys really discuss the environment for pricing, so I'd like to get some clarity on your thoughts there. And before doing that, Srinivas, can you just from a housekeeping perspective, I just want to clarify that you are now saying that a 60 basis point decline in operating margins, whereas, before you were saying 100 to 150 basis points. Is that correct? V. SRINIVAS: Not really. From the U.S. GAAP perspective, what I told earlier Julio is basically in the Indian GAAP there we have what we call the EBITDA. At the EBITDA level what we said is 60 basis points, earlier we said 100 basis points, now we are saying 60 basis points. Now coming to U.S. GAAP, you guys focus on EBIT. So if I want to talk about EBIT, year-on-year I think that is going to be kind of flattish. So we are not expecting any decline at the EBIT level, maybe it will be a flattish kind of a situation we are expecting. JULIO QUINTEROS: And before -- and what were you thinking before today? V. SRINIVAS: Before we were thinking it will be roughly around 40 to 50 basis points? JULIO QUINTEROS: Got it. Okay, thank you. OPERATOR: The next question is from Bryan Keane with Prudential. B. RAMALINGA RAJU: Before we do that should we answer Julio's first question on pricing? BRYAN KEANE, ANALYST, PRUDENTIAL EQUITY GROUP: Yes, sure. B. RAMALINGA RAJU: Unless you are not

interested any more Julio? I think in general, Julio, our experience is that the pricing environment is -- for a few quarters we have seen a fairly stable pricing environment. Also a pricing environment that is somewhat positive. We are positive about the potential for prices. That is backed up by our experience to date. The new customers that we are getting we are able to attract higher prices than our average pricing and that is roughly in the range of about 3 to 5% as far as average price increase is concerned. We are also seeing the increase in instances where we are able to renegotiate the existing contracts, not only as and when the contracts come up for renewal but also proactive renegotiation of contracts. And we are able to, in many instances, negotiate prices upwards for those contracts as well. So as far as average contracted prices are concerned, our experience is stable to positive as far as pricing is concerned. Now, we have mentioned earlier, what we need to do is convert that increase to a similar increase in realized prices. And there are a few variables that we have discussed earlier about how to manage that well. And our endeavor continues to be to manage that. And we remain fairly comfortable about the pricing environment, number one, it is remaining stable and, number two, it is [inaudible]. Yes. Can we move on to the next question please? BRYAN KEANE: Okay. It's Bryan Keane. I just wanted a follow up on the prior question about EBIT being more flattish now, verse it was expected to be more 40 to 50 basis points decline. What exactly are the reasons for the improvement that you are expecting? V. SRINIVAS: Whatever the improvements we have seen in Q3, which we talked about in terms of various operational efficiency and other cost optimization initiatives, have yielded to us in Q3. That is the primary reason for this. BRYAN KEANE: Okay. Is there a way to quantify the different levers there? V. SRINIVAS: I talked about it. We have levers like

ELTP. That is what we call broadening the associates pyramid, thereby, reducing the average cost of delivery. That is one very important, significant lever. Then we have better fixed bid project management, whereby, getting higher yield from each project, higher profitability from each project. And then we have other initiatives like employee rotation; this is between on-site and offshore. These are some of the levers we have, apart from of course the SG&A, controlling the SG&A. While this quarter we have seen some increase but we expect to control that and bring in some efficiencies there as well. BRYAN KEANE: Okay, yes that's helpful. I just wanted to get that down. And then my last question is on the demand environment. We've seen ERP vendors reported some weakness in sales. Do you guys see any weakness in the environment, I guess, both in U.S. and in Europe? RAM MYNAMPATI: Brian, this is Ram Mynampati here. In fact, as you can see our Consulting and Enterprise business solutions has reported increasing in this quarter [technical difficulty] as far as the revenue is concerned. In our Enterprise Solutions practice, obviously, its distributed among many products lines and many service lines, not just limited to one year [vendor]. While there is in certain parts by a few vendors about some slowdown in licensing, we don't see any specific impact on our business because our business is not entirely dependent on the volume of licenses. There are internal integration projects that we do. There are implementation projects that we do. In spite of the talk about some licensing slowdown, our view is that that is not going to impact our business negatively. BRYAN KEANE: Okay. Thanks a lot and good quarter. RAM MYNAMPATI: Thank you. OPERATOR: Ladies and gentlemen. Please limit your questions to one. The next question is from Rod Bourgeois of Bernstein. ROD BOURGEOIS, ANALYST, SANFORD BERNSTEIN: Hey guys. I just wanted to take a big-picture look at demand from a couple of different angles. Clearly, this is an important part of the year, as your clients start to reset budgets and

define their spending intentions for the next year. Are you picking up anything noteworthy from your clients about future spending intentions, as you talk to them about what they're going to do over the course of the next year? Is there any incrementally positive, or incrementally negative data points from those discussions, or it is for a normal course trajectory from what you can tell at this point? B. RAMALINGA RAJU: Rod, this is Ramalinga here. As we discussed with the media for the decision-makers, it is what I sense is a guarded optimism. So, to that end it is a relatively more positive environment related to IT solution spend that is being witnessed in the market. We heard mention of about 5 to 6% increase in IT solutions' budget. While there are some negatives that are somewhat skeptical about some slowdown in the market and [tough] lending and stuff like that. But the majority of our discussions seem to give us a confidence that IT budgets will experience a moderate increase. But what is clear in our discussions is that there is a greater desire on the part of many of the executives, to direct a significant portion of the spend towards global diluted model, rather than trying to control spending towards global diluted model. And we see that as a very positive sign. So, I have not picked up any specific negatives that [one-off] client situations that perhaps was impacted by a specific and unique business situation. But if I painted our picture of what we're hearing in the market, I would categorize that as the more positive than what we heard last year. ROD BOURGEOIS: Alright. And just related to that, question about the demand pipeline, are you seeing in your pipeline more of a shift towards larger deals? Or is it a similar mix as in the past of large deals [inaudible] projects? As I look at your client matrix, there's some indication that you're not really seeing a big shift towards larger deals at this point. And I'm wondering if the pipeline reflects the trend

that might be more big deal orientated that what you seen in the recent history? VENKATESH RODDAM: I would say this, Rod, that we have seen both. We are seeing very good interactions where we've got existing clients, indicating a good appetite to consider large schemes. We are also seeing good pipeline in large deals without the clients necessarily being our existing clients. So, we can just get large deals as a different area with a separate focus, because we see that pipeline very active and we are very -- very positively inclined in light of our experiences of operationalizing the large deals that we have won that we are fairly confident of being able to manage those deals well. So, the pipeline on the large deal side is certainly healthy. But we are also seeing the existing customers -- some of the large existing customers considering -- converting set up opportunities to an integrated fashion as in [R&D]. So, I would not necessarily say that these are mutually exclusive. I would say that there are a few customers that are fairly large customers of ours that are considering larger deals as the next course of action. ROD BOURGEOIS: Right, that's helpful. Thanks guys. VENKATESH RODDAM: Thank you. OPERATOR: Our next question is from Joseph Foresi of Janney Montgomery. JOSEPH FORESI, ANALYST, JANNEY MONTGOMERY SCOTT: Hi guys. My first question is sort of on the margin side. And just the first part of it's housekeeping. Did you say the RSU charge was 4.5m and that that's been moved to the fourth quarter? VENKATESH RODDAM: Yes. You're right. It doesn't move now, that will be coming in Q4. JOSEPH FORESI: Okay. And my second part of the margin question is, you guys have talked about flattening the employee pyramid and being able to reduce the overall costs of employees. I'm wondering if you guys could tell us, do you think you'll hit an inflection point where you'll actually start to see a benefit on the margins, or is that more of a catch-up type thing, where you're trying to just offset

your employee base versus the other one? So, in other words, next year could we see a benefit from that on the margin side? VENKATESH RODDAM: Yes. This broadening the associate pyramid is going to be an issue on which we are going to continue to focus on. And we have been focus on -- focusing on it for the last now, one year. And also we will definitely continue to focus on it next year as well. So, for the next [inaudible] the economies or the benefits to that -- and this initiative is going to [inaudible] will flow -- inflow to us even during the next year as well. JOSEPH FORESI: Okay. So, we haven't had an inflection point there. You still see some upside to that? VENKATESH RODDAM: No. Not really. JOSEPH FORESI: Okay. And just one last question if I could on the demand side. I know you guys talked about earlier in the call, there being four large deals that you guys have just signed for and there's some potential for large deals on the way. Are we seeing all four of those deals in the numbers or do you expect to ramp up two of them within the next two quarters? Could you just give us some clarity on that? And thanks again. V. SRINIVAS: All we said was that two of those large deals have ramped up enough to figure in the top 10. So, obviously, we have ramped up the other two also. But not appreciably large to have them figure in the top 10. So, that's only distinction. But we have obviously operationally [had] all the four deals. Two of them have actually kept efficiently to the [inaudible]. JOSEPH FORESI: So, I guess in a general sense then, can we expect to see the other two in the next 12 months? Is that usually how it works or is there more of a timeframe if you -- V. SRINIVAS: That's the expectation that the other two would see a ramp up in the next 12 months. So, it's very difficult to

put an actual timeframe because it could happen in two quarters as well. Obviously, that would get to a level of [BPN] related to planning that we feel we don't want to get into in this call. But it's a fair expectation that you'll see that in the next 12 months, yes. JOSEPH FORESI: Sure. I appreciate it guys. Thanks. V. SRINIVAS: Thank you. OPERATOR: The next question is from the line of George Price of Stifel Nicolaus. GEORGE PRICE, ANALYST, STIFEL NICOLAUS: Hi. Thanks for taking my question. Most of my questions have been answered but I would like to circle back around and push you if I could a little bit on one area. And that is just the near-term revenue growth outlook and specifically what we're seeing in the second half of fiscal '07 and in the quarter and what we're expecting in March. Notwithstanding the comments about projects having a natural end and timing and so forth, clearly, demand indicators have been very strong. The reports have been very strong and yet the revenue growth, while visually attractive, is still a little, I think, below expectations going into the March quarter. How, -- I guess can you give us a sense maybe of timing of the -- of some of these projects that have ended and the things you see ramping up? I still don't fully understand why maybe the revenue improvement shouldn't come sooner? B. RAMALINGA RAJU: This is Raju here. I would like to just remind you that last year we have registered highest growth in the industry. And last quarter, for example, we had close to about 10% growth [registered] sequentially. I'd like to just state that 7.7% growth is a fairly a healthy growth. It may not have matched the best in the industry. But then again, one should not draw conclusions based on what happens in just 60 working days in a quarter. We continue to be quite upbeat about the growth prospects. We have also stated, going forward, that it's not just about general volumes but the opportunities for improvement

in prices as well, because we have clearly entered a new environment of fairly sizeable deals and taking up of greater responsibility in many instances, and the level of business transformation exercises being carried out by us. VENKATESH RODDAM: It goes without saying that we may not be in a position to give any guidance for the next year. But all we are saying is that we find the environment positive and our [inaudible] well placed to reap the benefits from a positive marketplace as is [inaudible]. GEORGE PRICE: Okay. Thank you. I just have a specific question, maybe for Hari. What was the operating margin at Nipuna, and was it at all impacted by the 4K transaction? I know you had a large transaction and animation in the quarter. Thank you very much. V. SRINIVAS: This is Srinivas here. That is the reason why the EBITDA is [inaudible] came off a little bit quarter on quarter. Otherwise, we feel we kept the overall trend on a year-on-year basis. And definitely there is a

considerable improvement. On the revenue front, yes, there is an almost over 80% growth we are looking at year-on-year. On the EBITDA level, operating margin level last year there is a huge loss. So, overall, I think we've been asked for comments, there is a considerable improvement this year when compared to last year. the situation as well as the opportunity? Thank you. ASHISH THADANI: That's very helpful. Just one quick clarification, what percentage of your revenue actually comes from Fortune 500 type clients? VENKATESH RODDAM: We have 160 Fortune 500 clients that we work for. But we have not given out specific numbers for this segment. But it goes without saying that this is quite significant and it follows, as I have stated, the 80/20 principle. ASHISH THADANI: Fair enough. Thank

you very much. OPERATOR: Thank you. I'll hand the call back over to India. OPERATOR: Thank you very much Christine. Full text: OPERATOR: Good evening ladies and gentlemen. I am Pratibha, the moderator for this conference. Welcome to the Satyam Earnings Call. For the duration of the presentation, all participants' lines will be in the listen-only mode. Good morning and good evening to you all and thank you for joining us to discuss our third quarter results. Joining me on this call are Mr. B. Ramalinga Raju, Chairman of our Company and Mr. Ram Mynampati, President, Commercial and Healthcare Businesses, and we also have Prakash Challa, who is the CEO of our subsidiary -- BPO subsidiary Nipuna Services Limited. Before we start the discussions, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that during this call, we may make certain forward-looking statements concerning our future growth prospect. Such statements involve a number of risks and uncertainties associated with our business. Please refer to our various periodic filings with the SEC for the description of such risks. The company does not undertake to update any forward-looking statement that may be made from time-to-time by or on behalf of the company. I'll now hand over the session to Raju. competitor, while you have the same kind of a growth rate that Infosys has. VADLAMANI SRINIVAS: That is what I was saying, our R&P is almost now 80%, 75% to 80% of Infosys. RAMA RAO: Why is it so? RAMALINGA RAJU: We will not be able to comment on that. We believe that we have been able to perform well, and we have [inaudible] both at the top line level and bottom line level. We have [inaudible] our business, we have done relatively well on various fronts. There are few Indian companies that have done relatively well, and we believe we have built our own strength. We cannot comment on the market reactions to what we do, other than saying that we are doing our best to not only do well, but communicate what we do well enough to our stakeholders. We'll continue that effort. RAMA RAO: Thank you, very good. Good luck guys. OPERATOR: At this time there are no further questions.
